questions.stem: A 38-year-old landscaper comes to the occupational health clinic 10 minutes after a wasp sting on the forearm. The nurse notes a 3-cm raised, red, itchy wheal at the site. The client is anxious but talking in full sentences. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply a cool compress to the wheal to ease the itching
Give the prescribed oral antihistamine for the itching
Ask about throat tightness and listen for wheezing
Teach the client to avoid scratching the sting site
optionRationales: Incorrect. A cool compress is a reasonable comfort measure, but only after the airway and breathing are confirmed safe.
Incorrect. An antihistamine relieves histamine-driven itch but does not treat airway involvement, so assessment comes first.
Correct. The wheal shows local histamine release, but the nurse must first rule out body-wide mediator release affecting the airway and breathing.
Incorrect. Teaching is appropriate later; it does not address the possibility that the reaction is spreading.
questions.rationale: A wheal within minutes of a sting reflects mast cells in the skin releasing histamine, which dilates and leaks local vessels and triggers itching. The same mediators can be released throughout the body, so the nurse's first job is to look beyond the skin for airway, breathing, or circulation involvement. The cool compress and antihistamine are tempting because they match the visible problem, but they address comfort rather than safety. Once the airway and breathing are confirmed normal, local comfort measures and teaching follow.
questions.takeaway: With any mediator-driven skin reaction, check the airway and breathing before treating the itch.
questions.hintContent: Think about where else mast cells release the same mediators besides the skin.
questions.hintStrategy: When every option is reasonable, choose the assessment that rules out a life-threatening problem before comfort measures.

questions.stem: The nurse on a medical unit receives four call-light requests at the same time. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with new chest tightness and itching all over 10 minutes after starting IV cefazolin
A client with an ankle sprain who rates the throbbing pain 6/10 and is due for ibuprofen
A client with influenza who has body aches, a headache, and a temperature of 38.3 °C (100.9 °F)
A client with several mosquito bites on the legs who is asking for an anti-itch cream
optionRationales: Correct. Generalized itching plus chest tightness minutes after a new drug suggests body-wide mediator release reaching the airway, a possible early anaphylaxis.
Incorrect. Bradykinin- and prostaglandin-driven sprain pain needs treatment soon, but it is a stable, local problem.
Incorrect. Prostaglandin-driven fever and aches are expected with influenza and do not threaten the airway.
Incorrect. Local histamine-driven itching is uncomfortable but not dangerous.
questions.rationale: All four clients have mediator effects, but only one involves the airway. Itching all over plus chest tightness right after a new IV antibiotic suggests mast cells are releasing histamine and leukotrienes throughout the body, which can tighten airway smooth muscle and progress to anaphylaxis within minutes. The sprain is the most tempting distractor because 6/10 pain feels urgent, yet it is an expected local response in a stable client. Systemic mediator release after a drug exposure outranks local pain, fever, or itching.
questions.takeaway: Mediator release that is body-wide or involves the airway outranks local pain, fever, or itch.
questions.hintContent: Ask which mediator effect, in which location, could kill within minutes.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply the ABCs: the client with a possible airway or breathing threat is seen first.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old client has taken ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for 3 weeks for acute shoulder tendinitis, often on an empty stomach. Today the client reports burning epigastric pain and two black, tarry stools. BP is 118/72 mm Hg and HR is 94/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the next ibuprofen dose with a full meal and a glass of milk
Offer an antacid and reassess the epigastric pain in 1 hour
Suggest acetaminophen for the shoulder pain instead of ibuprofen
Hold the next ibuprofen dose and report the findings to the provider
optionRationales: Incorrect. Food helps prevent stomach irritation, but once bleeding signs appear, continuing the NSAID is unsafe.
Incorrect. An antacid may ease the burning, but it can mask symptoms and delays reporting a possible GI bleed.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen is a reasonable pain option that spares the stomach, but switching drugs does not get a possible GI bleed evaluated by the provider.
Correct. Black, tarry stools suggest upper GI bleeding; prostaglandins protect the stomach lining, and the drug blocking them should be stopped and the provider notified.
questions.rationale: Prostaglandins cause pain and fever at an injured site, but they also protect the stomach lining and help maintain kidney blood flow. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen block prostaglandin production, so heavy use without food can erode the stomach and cause bleeding, shown here by black, tarry stools. The most tempting distractor is giving the dose with food; food helps prevent irritation, but it does not make it safe to continue once bleeding is suspected. Holding the drug and notifying the provider protects the client.
questions.takeaway: Blocking prostaglandins removes their stomach protection; signs of GI bleeding on an NSAID mean hold and report.
questions.hintContent: Remember the protective jobs prostaglandins have outside the inflamed tissue.
questions.hintStrategy: When a finding signals harm from a drug, stop the harm before choosing ways to make the drug easier to tolerate.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. Refer to the Vital Signs. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document that the ibuprofen effectively reduced the fever
Apply oxygen per protocol and notify the provider of the low SpO₂
Encourage oral fluids to replace losses from the earlier fever
Recheck the temperature in 1 hour to confirm the fever is resolving
optionRationales: Incorrect. The fever did fall, so this is accurate documentation, but it ignores the falling SpO₂ and rising RR that need action now.
Correct. The SpO₂ has fallen and the respiratory rate has risen; this breathing problem needs action now despite the lower temperature.
Incorrect. Fluids are helpful, but they do not address hypoxemia, which is the immediate threat.
Incorrect. Rechecking shows the fever trend, but focusing on the temperature misses the worsening respiratory status.
questions.rationale: Ibuprofen lowers fever by blocking prostaglandins, which act on the hypothalamus to raise the body's temperature set point. It does not kill bacteria or treat the pneumonia, so a near-normal temperature can coexist with a worsening infection. Here the RR has climbed to 30 and the SpO₂ has dropped to 88%, signaling impaired gas exchange. The tempting choice is to call the ibuprofen a success, but evaluating the client by the thermometer alone ignores the breathing data that matter most.
questions.takeaway: An NSAID can bring a fever down without improving the infection; judge the client by breathing and oxygenation, not temperature alone.
questions.hintContent: Consider which signs ibuprofen changes and which signs it cannot touch.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare the rows: identify what improved, what worsened, and which change threatens the ABCs.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman arrives at urgent care with hives that began 20 minutes after eating at a new restaurant. Oral diphenhydramine was given 15 minutes ago. She now says, “The itching is better, but my tongue feels thick and my voice sounds funny.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give a second dose of diphenhydramine to complete the treatment
Give epinephrine IM per protocol and call for emergency help
Apply cool compresses to the hives and recheck her in 15 minutes
Check her oxygen saturation and listen for stridor
optionRationales: Incorrect. Antihistamines block only histamine and act too slowly to open a swelling airway.
Correct. A thick tongue and voice change mean airway swelling from body-wide mediator release; epinephrine reverses it.
Incorrect. Cool compresses soothe hives, but waiting 15 minutes allows the airway swelling to progress.
Incorrect. Assessing oxygenation and airway sounds is reasonable, but a thick tongue and voice change already show airway swelling; assessing first delays epinephrine.
questions.rationale: Antihistamines block one mediator, histamine, so they relieve itching and hives. In a reaction that spreads beyond the skin, many mediators are released at once, and capillary leak swells the tongue and larynx. The improving itch is the tempting cue because it suggests the treatment is working, but the new voice change shows the airway is now involved. Epinephrine IM constricts vessels and reduces swelling, so it comes first.
questions.takeaway: Better itching on an antihistamine does not mean the reaction is controlled; any airway sign means epinephrine now.
questions.hintContent: Think about what an antihistamine can and cannot block.
questions.hintStrategy: When a new airway finding appears, it overrides earlier signs of improvement.

questions.stem: A parent calls the pediatric clinic nurse line. The parent's 4-year-old was stung by a bee on the hand 10 minutes ago. The hand has a red, itchy welt, and the child is now coughing and has puffy lips. Which instruction should the nurse give first?
options: Give an oral antihistamine and call back if the cough gets worse
Put ice on the sting site and watch her closely for an hour
Drive her to the nearest emergency department right away
Call 911 now and use her epinephrine auto-injector if she has one
optionRationales: Incorrect. This delays epinephrine and emergency care while the airway may be closing.
Incorrect. Ice eases the local sting reaction, but it ignores the cough and lip swelling that signal airway involvement.
Incorrect. She does need emergency care, but driving delays epinephrine and leaves no one to manage her airway on the way; EMS brings treatment to her.
Correct. Coughing and lip swelling show mediators are acting on the airway; outside the hospital this needs EMS and epinephrine immediately.
questions.rationale: A welt at the sting site is a local histamine response, but cough and lip swelling show mast cells are releasing mediators beyond the sting, swelling and narrowing the airway. Outside the hospital, the priority is activating EMS and giving epinephrine immediately. The antihistamine option is tempting because the child is small and the welt itches, but antihistamines act slowly and cannot reverse airway swelling. Every minute of delay increases the risk of airway closure.
questions.takeaway: Airway signs after a sting at home mean call 911 and give epinephrine; never wait and see with an antihistamine.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether the reaction is still local or has spread to another body system.
questions.hintStrategy: In telephone triage, choose the instruction that gets emergency care moving fastest when the ABCs are threatened.

questions.stem: A client is 3 days post-op after open reduction of a forearm fracture and receives scheduled ibuprofen every 6 hours. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F). The client reports incisional pain that is worse than yesterday, and the dressing has a small amount of thick, cloudy drainage. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Report the drainage and pain; ibuprofen may be masking a fever
Recheck the temperature in 4 hours to look for a fever
Give the scheduled ibuprofen and reassess the pain in 1 hour
Change the dressing and recheck the incision in 24 hours
optionRationales: Correct. Worsening pain and purulent drainage suggest infection; blocking prostaglandins can blunt the fever that would usually accompany it.
Incorrect. Trending the temperature is reasonable, but around-the-clock ibuprofen can keep it down, and waiting delays reporting clear local signs of infection.
Incorrect. Scheduled pain relief is appropriate, but it treats the symptom only and does not get the cloudy drainage evaluated.
Incorrect. A dressing change lets the nurse inspect the wound, but waiting 24 hours delays evaluation of a likely wound infection.
questions.rationale: Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandins, which drive both fever and pain, so scheduled doses can blunt the cues a nurse relies on to detect infection. Increasing incisional pain and thick, cloudy drainage are signs of a possible wound infection even with a near-normal temperature. The tempting distractor is waiting for a fever to appear, but the thermometer is unreliable while prostaglandins are blocked. The nurse reports the drainage and pain promptly so the wound can be evaluated.
questions.takeaway: An NSAID can hide fever and pain; trust local signs such as purulent drainage and worsening pain.
questions.hintContent: Think about which signs of infection depend on prostaglandins.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for a medication in the stem that could be changing the data you are given.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client with an acute, painful knee injury has taken ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours for 4 days. Refer to the Kidney Data. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Encourage the client to drink an extra 2 liters of fluid throughout today
Give the ibuprofen with food to protect the kidneys
Hold the ibuprofen and notify the provider of the kidney findings
Start strict intake and output and report at the end of the shift
optionRationales: Incorrect. Extra fluid does not remove the cause, and low urine output raises the risk of fluid overload.
Incorrect. Taking ibuprofen with food is sound advice, but food protects the stomach lining, not the kidneys.
Correct. Prostaglandins help maintain kidney blood flow; blocking them can reduce kidney perfusion, especially in older adults.
Incorrect. Strict intake and output is useful monitoring, but the creatinine has already doubled and output is very low; waiting until shift end delays holding the drug.
questions.rationale: Besides causing pain and fever, prostaglandins help maintain blood flow to the kidneys. NSAIDs block prostaglandin production, which can reduce kidney perfusion, and older adults are especially vulnerable. A creatinine that has doubled, a rising BUN, and urine output of about 17 mL/hr signal kidney harm. Giving the drug with food is tempting because it is standard NSAID teaching, but food protects the stomach, not the kidneys; the drug should be held and the provider notified.
questions.takeaway: NSAIDs remove prostaglandins' support of kidney blood flow; falling urine output and rising creatinine mean hold and report.
questions.hintContent: Prostaglandins have a protective job in the kidneys, too.
questions.hintStrategy: Trend the data across columns; a doubled value plus low output signals harm that needs action, not more monitoring.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old soccer player had an elastic wrap applied in triage for an ankle sprain 1 hour ago. The ankle is now markedly swollen, and the client reports numb toes, which are pale and cool with a capillary refill of 4 seconds. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply an ice pack over the wrap to reduce the swelling
Give the prescribed ibuprofen to reduce the inflammation
Raise the ankle on two pillows so it is above heart level
Loosen the elastic wrap and reassess circulation to the toes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Ice helps swelling over time but leaves the compression in place.
Incorrect. Ibuprofen takes time to work and does not relieve the immediate compression.
Incorrect. With circulation already impaired, raising the limb above the heart can cut arterial flow further; loosen the wrap and keep the ankle at heart level.
Correct. Fluid leaking from permeable vessels is swelling the ankle inside a fixed wrap, compressing vessels and nerves.
questions.rationale: Histamine and bradykinin make vessels leaky, and the escaping fluid swells the injured tissue. When swelling expands inside a fixed wrap, the pressure compresses vessels and nerves, causing pale, cool, numb toes with slow refill. The nurse removes the cause of compression first and then reassesses. Elevation is the most tempting distractor because it is part of standard sprain care, but it cannot restore blood flow while the wrap is still too tight, and raising a limb with poor circulation can reduce arterial flow further, so the ankle stays at heart level until perfusion returns.
questions.takeaway: When inflammatory swelling compromises circulation, loosen the constriction first and keep the limb at heart level, not above it.
questions.hintContent: Swelling has nowhere to go inside something tight.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the action that removes the cause of the problem before options that only ease it.

questions.stem: On a pediatric unit, the RN asks a UAP to apply cool compresses to a 6-year-old's itchy, local insect-bite welts. Which instruction to the UAP is most important?
options: “Give her the antihistamine if the itching keeps her awake.”
“Listen to her lungs every hour and let me know about any wheezing.”
“Tell me right away if she starts wheezing or her lips swell.”
“Switch to a warm pack if the cool compress isn't helping.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Medication administration is not within the UAP's scope.
Incorrect. Auscultation is an assessment, which the RN must perform.
Correct. Reporting signs of spreading mediator release is within UAP scope and protects the child's airway.
Incorrect. Warmth increases vasodilation and can worsen histamine-driven itching and swelling.
questions.rationale: Local welts are a histamine response from skin mast cells, and cool compresses for comfort can be delegated. The key safety risk is that the reaction spreads, so the UAP must know which observations to report immediately: wheezing, lip or tongue swelling, or a hoarse voice. Listening to the lungs is tempting because it targets the same danger, but assessment belongs to the RN. Medication administration is also outside UAP scope.
questions.takeaway: When delegating care of a local allergic reaction, tell the UAP exactly which airway signs to report at once.
questions.hintContent: Identify the most dangerous way this local reaction could change.
questions.hintStrategy: For delegation items, choose the instruction that is within the UAP's scope and targets the biggest safety risk.

questions.stem: At a summer day camp, a 9-year-old develops raised, itchy welts within minutes of several mosquito bites. The child's grandmother asks why the bites itch and swell so quickly. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “White blood cells travel to the bites over several hours and form the welts.”
“Skin cells release histamine within seconds, which leaks small vessels and causes itch.”
“The mosquito injected bacteria, and the welts are an early skin infection.”
“Prostaglandins raise the skin temperature, and the heat is what causes itching.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. WBC recruitment is a slower step; the immediate welt and itch come from histamine.
Correct. Mast cells already in the skin release histamine within seconds, producing redness, swelling, and itch.
Incorrect. Welts within minutes are a mediator response, not an infection.
Incorrect. Prostaglandins cause pain and fever; itching and hives are histamine effects.
questions.rationale: Mast cells are stationed in the skin, packed with histamine and heparin, and they release them within seconds when triggered. Histamine dilates small vessels (redness), increases permeability (swelling), and stimulates itching, producing a wheal. The WBC option is tempting because WBCs are part of inflammation, but leukotriene-driven recruitment takes longer. Recognizing histamine as the immediate cause also guides comfort care, such as a cool compress or a prescribed antihistamine.
questions.takeaway: Itching and wheals within minutes point to mast-cell histamine.
questions.hintContent: Which cells are already waiting in the skin, and what do they hold?
questions.hintStrategy: Match the timing in the stem (seconds to minutes) to the mediator that acts that fast.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old client has an infected cut on the palm from a fishhook 2 days ago. The wound is red and swollen with a small amount of yellow pus. The client asks, “Where does the pus come from?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Leukotrienes call white blood cells to the cut; pus is those cells plus debris.”
“Heparin keeps blood flowing, and pus is the old blood breaking down.”
“Bradykinin makes the area painful, and the pain turns the fluid yellow.”
“Histamine forms small hives under the skin that break open and drain.”
optionRationales: Correct. Leukotrienes attract neutrophils and macrophages; the collection of dead cells, microbes, and debris forms pus.
Incorrect. Heparin prevents clotting at the site; pus is made of WBCs and debris, not old blood.
Incorrect. Bradykinin causes pain and leakage but does not create pus.
Incorrect. Hives are histamine wheals; they do not produce pus.
questions.rationale: Leukotrienes attract neutrophils and macrophages to the site, laying down the chemical trail (chemotaxis) that WBCs follow out of the vessels. As many WBCs gather and destroy bacteria, the collection of dead cells, microbes, and debris forms pus. The heparin option is tempting because heparin is released at the site, but its job is to prevent clotting and keep blood flowing. Recognizing pus as evidence of WBC recruitment helps the nurse identify an active infection that needs monitoring.
questions.takeaway: WBCs gathering in a wound, and the pus they form, reflect leukotriene recruitment.
questions.hintContent: Which mediator's specialty is calling in neutrophils and macrophages?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that pair a mediator with the wrong signature effect.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old client with an acutely inflamed, swollen knee after a fall started scheduled ibuprofen 2 days ago. Which finding best indicates that the drug's anti-prostaglandin effect is working?
options: The skin over the knee no longer itches when the client is resting
The client's temperature has stayed at 37.0 °C (98.6 °F)
Pain has decreased from 8/10 to 3/10, and the knee is less swollen
The client reports sleeping well with the knee raised on a pillow
optionRationales: Incorrect. Itching is a histamine effect, which ibuprofen does not block.
Incorrect. Ibuprofen does lower fever, but this client had no fever, so a normal temperature does not show the drug is working on the knee.
Correct. Prostaglandins drive pain, vasodilation, and leakage; less pain and swelling show reduced prostaglandin activity.
Incorrect. Better sleep may reflect comfort, but it is indirect and could come from elevation; less pain and swelling directly measure the drug's effect.
questions.rationale: Evaluate a drug by checking the problems it was given to fix. Ibuprofen blocks the COX enzyme so less prostaglandin is made, which means less pain, less vasodilation and leakage, and less fever. A drop in pain and swelling is the expected therapeutic effect. Loss of itching is tempting because it sounds like less inflammation, but itching is driven by histamine, which ibuprofen does not block.
questions.takeaway: Ibuprofen works by lowering prostaglandins, so evaluate it by pain, swelling, and fever.
questions.hintContent: Link the drug's target mediator to that mediator's signature effects.
questions.hintStrategy: For 'effective' questions, choose the finding that matches the drug's mechanism.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 41-year-old client with a severe sunburn about the prescribed ibuprofen. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “This medicine will kill the germs causing my sunburn.”
“I'll take each dose with food or a glass of milk.”
“It lowers the chemicals that cause my pain and swelling.”
“I'll call if I notice black stools or stomach pain.”
optionRationales: Correct. This needs correcting: ibuprofen lowers prostaglandins and has no antibacterial action, and a sunburn involves no germs.
Incorrect. This is accurate; food helps protect the stomach lining that prostaglandins normally guard.
Incorrect. This is accurate; ibuprofen reduces prostaglandin production.
Incorrect. This is accurate; these can signal GI bleeding from prostaglandin blockade.
questions.rationale: Ibuprofen is an NSAID that blocks prostaglandin production, reducing pain, swelling, and fever. It does not kill microorganisms, block histamine, or turn off the immune system, and claims like these are classic misconceptions. A sunburn is inflammation from a physical agent, with no germs involved. The other statements are accurate: food protects the stomach because prostaglandins normally help guard its lining, and black stools could signal bleeding.
questions.takeaway: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandins; they do not kill germs.
questions.hintContent: Recall what an NSAID blocks and what it does not do.
questions.hintStrategy: In 'needs further teaching' items, look for the false statement; the true statements are the distractors.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 30-year-old client with a fresh wrist sprain says, “I have allergy pills at home. Will those help the swelling and throbbing pain?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Yes, allergy pills block all of the chemicals that cause swelling and pain.”
“Allergy pills work best because histamine is the main cause of sprain pain.”
“Neither will help, because only an antibiotic can reduce sprain swelling.”
“Those block histamine, but sprain pain comes mostly from bradykinin and prostaglandins.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Antihistamines block only histamine, not every mediator.
Incorrect. Histamine mainly causes itching and leakage; sprain pain is driven by bradykinin and prostaglandins.
Incorrect. A sprain is not an infection; antibiotics do not affect inflammatory mediators.
Correct. Bradykinin stimulates pain nerves and prostaglandins sensitize them; antihistamines do not block either.
questions.rationale: Each mediator has a specialty. Bradykinin directly stimulates pain nerves, prostaglandins make those nerves more sensitive, and both add to vessel leakage and swelling. Antihistamines block only histamine, so they relieve itching and hives but do little for sprain pain. The tempting idea that an antihistamine treats all inflammation is a common misconception; a drug that lowers prostaglandins, such as an NSAID, is the better match.
questions.takeaway: Antihistamines treat itch and hives; bradykinin and prostaglandin pain needs a different approach.
questions.hintContent: Which mediators specialize in pain?
questions.hintStrategy: When a client proposes a drug, check whether its target mediator actually causes the symptom.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with influenza has a temperature of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F) and diffuse muscle aches. His daughter asks why the flu makes him feverish. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Histamine released in his muscles produces heat that spreads through the body.”
“Prostaglandins made during inflammation turn up the brain's temperature set point.”
“Heparin keeps his blood flowing so fast that his whole body overheats.”
“His white blood cells are burning energy and making the extra heat directly.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Histamine dilates and leaks local vessels and causes itching; it does not reset temperature.
Correct. Prostaglandins act on the hypothalamus to raise the set point, producing fever, and also sensitize pain nerves.
Incorrect. Heparin prevents clotting at injured sites; it does not cause fever.
Incorrect. Fever comes from a reset thermostat, not from heat produced by WBCs.
questions.rationale: Prostaglandins act on the hypothalamus, the brain's thermostat, and turn the set point up, producing fever; they also sensitize pain nerves, contributing to body aches. This is why one dose of an NSAID can lower fever and ease aches together. The WBC-heat option is tempting because WBCs are busy fighting the virus, but fever results from the reset thermostat. Histamine and heparin act on local vessels and clotting, not on temperature control.
questions.takeaway: Fever comes from prostaglandins resetting the hypothalamus.
questions.hintContent: Think about which mediator signals the brain's thermostat.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the symptom to the mediator's signature effect, and eliminate mediators whose job is local.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old client visits a friend who has two cats. Within minutes, the client has itchy, watery eyes, sneezing, and a runny nose. Lungs are clear, the voice is normal, and BP is 124/78 mm Hg. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: Anaphylaxis that requires IM epinephrine right now
A local allergic reaction from mast-cell histamine release
An acute bacterial infection of the eyes and nose
A viral respiratory infection caught from the friend
optionRationales: Incorrect. Anaphylaxis involves sudden body-wide signs such as airway swelling, wheezing, or hypotension, none of which are present.
Correct. Itching, watery eyes, and sneezing with normal airway, breathing, and BP fit a small, local mediator release.
Incorrect. Symptoms within minutes of an allergen exposure are a mediator response, not an infection.
Incorrect. A virus would not cause symptoms within minutes of exposure.
questions.rationale: When an allergen triggers a small, local mediator release, mast cells in the eyes and nose release histamine, producing itching, tearing, sneezing, and a runny nose. Clear lungs, a normal voice, and a normal BP show that the airway, breathing, and circulation are not involved, so this is not anaphylaxis. The anaphylaxis option is tempting because an allergen is present, but anaphylaxis requires sudden involvement of the airway, breathing, or circulation, or of two or more body systems. The nurse still teaches the client to watch for those signs.
questions.takeaway: Local itching, sneezing, and tearing with normal ABCs is a local allergic reaction; body-wide signs mean anaphylaxis.
questions.hintContent: Check whether any finding involves the airway, breathing, or circulation.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the normal findings in the stem to rule out the most dangerous option.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 16-year-old with allergic asthma had chest tightness and wheezing while cleaning a dusty basement. After the prescribed rescue inhaler, the wheezing has resolved. The teen asks why dust makes the airways tight. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Bradykinin from the dust stimulates pain nerves deep inside your lungs.”
“Heparin thins your blood, so less oxygen is able to reach your lungs.”
“Complement proteins plug your small airways with thick, sticky mucus.”
“Mast cells release leukotrienes that tighten the muscles around your airways.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Bradykinin's specialty is pain; it is not the main cause of airway tightening.
Incorrect. Heparin prevents clotting at injured sites and does not narrow the airways.
Incorrect. Complement helps dilation and phagocytosis; it does not plug airways.
Correct. Leukotrienes add to leakage and tighten airway smooth muscle, a key reason allergic reactions cause wheezing.
questions.rationale: When an allergen such as dust triggers airway mast cells, they release mediators that include histamine and leukotrienes. Leukotrienes attract WBCs, add to vessel leakiness, and cause airway smooth muscle to tighten, which narrows the airways and produces wheezing. The bradykinin option is tempting because the teen describes chest discomfort, but bradykinin's main job is pain, not bronchoconstriction. Understanding the trigger supports teaching about avoiding dust exposure.
questions.takeaway: Allergic wheezing reflects mast-cell mediators such as leukotrienes tightening airway smooth muscle.
questions.hintContent: Which mediator acts on airway smooth muscle as well as calling in WBCs?
questions.hintStrategy: Link the body location in the stem (airways) to the mediator known to act there.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 55-year-old client takes aspirin for tension headaches. In the spring she says, “Aspirin fixes my headaches and fevers, so why doesn't it stop my itchy, watery allergy eyes?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Aspirin lowers prostaglandins, but allergy itching is caused by histamine.”
“You probably need a higher aspirin dose to block the allergy chemicals.”
“Aspirin only works on infections, and allergies are not an infection.”
“Aspirin blocks histamine only in the brain, not in the eyes or nose.”
optionRationales: Correct. Aspirin blocks prostaglandin production; allergic itching is a histamine effect that it does not affect.
Incorrect. More aspirin will not block histamine and increases the risk of stomach bleeding.
Incorrect. Aspirin reduces prostaglandins; it has no antimicrobial action.
Incorrect. Aspirin does not block histamine anywhere; it lowers prostaglandins.
questions.rationale: Aspirin is a salicylate that blocks the COX enzyme, so less prostaglandin is made, relieving pain and fever. Allergic itching and watering of the eyes are caused by histamine released from mast cells, a different mediator that aspirin does not block. The higher-dose option is tempting because the client believes the drug is simply too weak, but no dose of aspirin blocks histamine, and higher doses raise the risk of stomach injury. Matching the symptom to its mediator explains why different drugs are needed.
questions.takeaway: Aspirin and NSAIDs block prostaglandins (pain, fever); antihistamines block histamine (itch, hives).
questions.hintContent: Name the mediator behind each of her symptoms.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client asks why a drug helps one symptom but not another, look for an answer that names two different mediators.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old lifeguard comes to the campus health office with a painful, red, warm sunburn across the shoulders and back. There are no blisters, and vital signs are normal. The client asks for help with the pain and swelling. Which prescribed medication best targets the cause of these symptoms?
options: Diphenhydramine taken at bedtime
Acetaminophen every 6 hours
Ibuprofen taken with food
Lidocaine gel on the skin
optionRationales: Incorrect. Diphenhydramine blocks histamine and itching but does not reduce prostaglandin-driven pain.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen relieves pain, but it has little anti-inflammatory effect, so it does not reduce the prostaglandin-driven swelling and redness.
Correct. Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin production, reducing the vasodilation, pain, and swelling of acute inflammation.
Incorrect. Topical lidocaine numbs the burned skin for comfort, but it does not reduce the prostaglandin-driven inflammation causing the symptoms.
questions.rationale: A sunburn is acute inflammation caused by a physical agent, ultraviolet light, with no infection involved. The redness, warmth, pain, and swelling are driven largely by prostaglandins, which cause vasodilation, sensitize pain nerves, and add to permeability. Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin production and is taken with food to protect the stomach. Diphenhydramine is tempting because it is a familiar 'anti-reaction' drug, but it blocks only histamine and does little for pain.
questions.takeaway: For inflammatory pain and swelling, choose the drug that lowers prostaglandins.
questions.hintContent: Identify the mediator behind pain and swelling, then the drug class that blocks it.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that treat a cause not present in the stem, such as infection.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old client with influenza has a temperature of 38.9 °C (102 °F), a headache, muscle aches, and a dry cough. The client is prescribed ibuprofen. Which effects should the nurse expect the ibuprofen to produce? Select all that apply.
options: Relief of the muscle aches
A shorter time that the client is contagious
Destruction of the influenza virus
A lower temperature
Relief of the headache
optionRationales: Correct. Body aches are partly prostaglandin-driven and should ease.
Incorrect. Ibuprofen does not affect the virus or how long the client can spread it.
Incorrect. NSAIDs have no antiviral or antimicrobial action.
Correct. Prostaglandins raise the hypothalamic set point; blocking them lowers the fever.
Correct. Prostaglandins sensitize pain nerves, so lowering them eases headache pain.
questions.rationale: Ibuprofen blocks the COX enzyme, so less prostaglandin is produced. Because prostaglandins drive fever, pain, and aches, the nurse expects all three to improve. Ibuprofen does not kill microorganisms or shorten the illness, so infection-control teaching still applies. The tempting error is assuming that feeling better means the infection is gone; the client remains contagious even when the fever is controlled.
questions.takeaway: NSAIDs relieve prostaglandin-driven fever, pain, and aches; they do not treat the infection.
questions.hintContent: List the signature effects of prostaglandins.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it is a prostaglandin effect; select only those.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 46-year-old warehouse worker with an acute shoulder strain who is starting ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: The drug eases pain and swelling by lowering prostaglandins
Report black, tarry stools or stomach pain
The drug will stop any itching caused by the strain
The drug helps prevent infection in the injured shoulder
Take a double dose if the pain is not relieved in an hour
Take each dose with food or milk
optionRationales: Correct. This accurately explains the mechanism of an NSAID.
Correct. These can signal GI bleeding caused by loss of prostaglandin protection.
Incorrect. Itching is a histamine effect; NSAIDs do not block histamine.
Incorrect. NSAIDs have no antimicrobial action, and a strain is not an infection.
Incorrect. Doubling the dose increases the risk of stomach and kidney injury.
Correct. Prostaglandins help protect the stomach lining; food reduces irritation when they are blocked.
questions.rationale: Teaching about an NSAID should explain how it works and how to use it safely. It reduces pain and swelling by lowering prostaglandin production, but because prostaglandins also protect the stomach lining and support kidney blood flow, doses are taken with food and signs of GI bleeding are reported. NSAIDs do not prevent infection or block histamine. Doubling a dose is tempting for a client in pain, but it raises the risk of harm without addressing the cause.
questions.takeaway: NSAID teaching: take with food, report GI bleeding, and expect relief of pain and swelling, not infection control.
questions.hintContent: Consider both what prostaglandins do at the injury and what they protect elsewhere.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each option as true or false on its own; reject any that claim antimicrobial or antihistamine effects.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old client develops anaphylaxis minutes after a bee sting. Which findings are correctly matched with the mediator action that causes them? Select all that apply.
options: Lip and tongue swelling from capillary leak
BP 82/50 mm Hg from widespread vasodilation
Bleeding gums from the release of heparin
Wheezing from tightening of airway smooth muscle
Fever of 39 °C from prostaglandins resetting the thermostat
optionRationales: Correct. Leaky capillaries let fluid escape into the tissues, swelling the lips, tongue, and throat.
Correct. Body-wide dilation of vessels lowers vascular resistance and blood pressure.
Incorrect. Heparin acts locally to keep blood flowing; bleeding gums are not a sign of anaphylaxis.
Correct. Mediators such as leukotrienes and histamine narrow the airways, producing wheezing.
Incorrect. Fever is not a feature of anaphylaxis, which develops over minutes.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis is the same set of mediator actions seen in local inflammation, released body-wide at once. Widespread vasodilation drops the BP, capillary leak swells the lips, tongue, and throat and pulls fluid out of the bloodstream, and airway smooth muscle tightening causes wheezing. The heparin and fever options are tempting because heparin and prostaglandins are real mediators, but their effects do not explain the findings of anaphylaxis. Understanding these mechanisms explains why epinephrine, which constricts vessels and opens the airways, is first-line.
questions.takeaway: Anaphylaxis is local inflammation gone body-wide: vasodilation drops BP, leak swells the airway, and smooth muscle tightening causes wheezing.
questions.hintContent: Picture what vasodilation, leakage, and airway tightening would look like if they happened everywhere at once.
questions.hintStrategy: Check both halves of each option: the finding must belong to anaphylaxis, and the mechanism must be correct.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old client with a bacterial skin abscess asks how a group of more than 20 circulating blood proteins helps the body fight the bacteria. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: “They reset the brain's thermostat to produce a fever.”
“They help call white blood cells to the infected area.”
“They coat the bacteria so white blood cells can recognize and engulf them.”
“They help widen and leak nearby vessels, partly by triggering mast cells.”
“They directly stimulate the pain nerves around the abscess.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Resetting the hypothalamic set point is a prostaglandin effect.
Correct. Complement contributes to attracting WBCs to the site.
Correct. Complement tags microbes, making phagocytosis easier.
Correct. Complement aids dilation and permeability, partly by causing histamine release.
Incorrect. Directly stimulating pain nerves is bradykinin's specialty.
questions.rationale: Complement is a group of more than 20 plasma proteins that circulate inactive and switch on in a chain when they meet microbes or injury. They aid dilation and permeability, partly by triggering mast cells, coat bacteria so WBCs can grab them (supporting phagocytosis), help call WBCs to the site, and can even punch holes in some bacteria. Pain and fever are tempting because the client with an abscess has both, but those are bradykinin and prostaglandin effects. Explaining complement accurately helps the client understand how the body clears an infection.
questions.takeaway: Complement tags microbes for phagocytosis, aids dilation, and helps recruit WBCs.
questions.hintContent: Think of complement as the tagging system for the WBC clean-up crew.
questions.hintStrategy: Assign each statement to the mediator that owns that effect; keep only those that belong to complement.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old client with an acute wrist injury is prescribed ibuprofen. While reconciling the client's home medications, the nurse looks for other drugs that also lower prostaglandin production so duplicate or added GI risk can be reported. Which home medications should the nurse identify? Select all that apply.
options: Diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime
Prednisone 10 mg daily
Aspirin 325 mg daily
Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily
Naproxen 220 mg as needed
Loratadine 10 mg daily
optionRationales: Incorrect. Diphenhydramine is an antihistamine and does not lower prostaglandins.
Correct. Corticosteroids also suppress prostaglandin production and add to GI risk with NSAIDs.
Correct. Aspirin is a salicylate that blocks COX and lowers prostaglandins.
Incorrect. Amoxicillin is an antibiotic and does not affect prostaglandins.
Correct. Naproxen is an NSAID and blocks prostaglandin production like ibuprofen.
Incorrect. Loratadine is an antihistamine; it blocks histamine, not prostaglandins.
questions.rationale: Salicylates (aspirin), NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen), and corticosteroids all reduce prostaglandin production, which is why they relieve pain, fever, and swelling. Because prostaglandins also protect the stomach lining, combining these drugs raises the risk of GI bleeding, so the nurse reports the combination. Antihistamines are tempting because they are also used for reactions and comfort, but they block histamine only. Antibiotics have no effect on mediators.
questions.takeaway: Aspirin, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids all lower prostaglandins; antihistamines and antibiotics do not.
questions.hintContent: Sort each drug by the mediator it targets.
questions.hintStrategy: Group the options by drug class first, then decide which classes share the mechanism.

questions.stem: At a family picnic, a 31-year-old is stung by a yellow jacket on the ankle. Twenty minutes later, the nurse assesses the client. Which findings indicate that mediator release has spread beyond the sting site and require immediate action? Select all that apply.
options: Warmth and mild swelling around the sting
A 2-cm red, itchy wheal at the sting site
Hives spreading across the chest and back
New hoarseness and a feeling of throat tightness
Dizziness with a BP of 86/50 mm Hg
optionRationales: Incorrect. Local vasodilation and leakage at the sting are expected.
Incorrect. A wheal at the sting is an expected local histamine response.
Correct. Generalized hives show histamine release far from the sting.
Correct. Upper airway swelling from capillary leak is an emergency sign.
Correct. Widespread vasodilation is lowering blood pressure.
questions.rationale: A sting normally causes a local response: mast cells at the site release histamine, producing a red, warm, itchy, swollen wheal. When mediators are released body-wide, findings appear far from the site or in other systems: generalized hives (skin), hoarseness and throat tightness (airway), and dizziness with hypotension (circulation). These indicate anaphylaxis and require epinephrine and emergency help. Local warmth and swelling are tempting because they are real inflammation, but they are expected at the sting.
questions.takeaway: Findings far from the sting or in the airway or circulation mean mediator release has gone body-wide.
questions.hintContent: Separate what is happening at the sting site from what is happening elsewhere.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask of each finding: is it at the site (expected) or in another place or body system (danger)?

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for several clients on a medical-surgical unit. Which findings are correctly paired with the mediator mainly responsible? Select all that apply.
options: Bacteria tagged for engulfment by WBCs: bradykinin
Fever and body aches with influenza: prostaglandins
An itchy wheal minutes after a mosquito bite: histamine
Throbbing pain of a fresh sprain: complement
Neutrophils gathering in an infected cut: leukotrienes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Tagging bacteria for phagocytosis is the job of complement, not bradykinin.
Correct. Prostaglandins reset the hypothalamic thermostat and sensitize pain nerves.
Correct. Mast-cell histamine causes local leakage and itching within seconds.
Incorrect. Sprain pain is driven mainly by bradykinin and prostaglandins, not complement.
Correct. Leukotrienes attract neutrophils and macrophages to the site.
questions.rationale: Each mediator has a signature effect. Prostaglandins cause vasodilation, pain, and fever; leukotrienes recruit neutrophils and macrophages; histamine causes rapid leakage, itching, and hives; bradykinin causes pain, dilation, and leakage; and complement tags microbes and aids phagocytosis. The two false pairings swap bradykinin and complement, a common mix-up because both are made from plasma proteins. Matching the finding to its mediator is the skill needed to predict which drug will help.
questions.takeaway: Histamine = itch and hives; bradykinin = pain; complement = tagging for phagocytosis; leukotrienes = WBC recruitment; prostaglandins = pain and fever.
questions.hintContent: Recall the one signature job of each mediator.
questions.hintStrategy: Read each pair as a true/false statement, and watch for two mediators that have been swapped.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old client developed itchy hives on the forearms after using a new laundry detergent. Vital signs are normal, the client has no airway or GI symptoms, and the client also has a mild tension headache. One hour after a prescribed dose of oral diphenhydramine, which findings indicate that the drug had its expected effect? Select all that apply.
options: The client's temperature has returned to normal
The raised wheals on the forearms are fading
The client's WBC count has decreased
The client's tension headache has resolved
The client reports that the itching has decreased
optionRationales: Incorrect. Fever is a prostaglandin effect, and the client did not have a fever.
Correct. Blocking histamine reduces local leakage, so hives fade.
Incorrect. An antihistamine does not lower the WBC count.
Incorrect. Headache pain is driven mainly by prostaglandins, not histamine, so an antihistamine is not expected to relieve it.
Correct. Diphenhydramine blocks histamine, the mediator that causes itching.
questions.rationale: Antihistamines such as diphenhydramine block histamine, the mast-cell mediator that causes itching and hives in a local allergic reaction. The expected outcomes are less itching and fading wheals. Antihistamines do not affect prostaglandin-driven pain or fever, and they do not change the WBC count. The pain option is tempting because the client feels better overall, but it does not reflect the drug's mechanism.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate an antihistamine by itching and hives, the effects of histamine.
questions.hintContent: Link the drug to the one mediator it blocks.
questions.hintStrategy: For evaluation items, select only outcomes that the drug's mechanism can produce.

questions.stem: The nurse in an orthopedic clinic reviews the charts of five clients who are each requesting an NSAID for acute pain. Which clients have the greatest risk of harm from blocking prostaglandin production and need the provider's review before an NSAID is given? Select all that apply.
options: A 38-year-old who had hives and wheezing after taking aspirin
A healthy 25-year-old who will take a short course with meals
A 79-year-old whose recent creatinine was 1.9 mg/dL
A 52-year-old with a peptic ulcer that bled last year
A 30-year-old with seasonal allergic rhinitis controlled by loratadine
optionRationales: Correct. NSAIDs are a listed trigger of anaphylaxis, and a reaction to aspirin suggests risk with related drugs.
Incorrect. A brief course with food in a healthy young adult carries low risk.
Correct. Prostaglandins support kidney blood flow; an older adult with reduced kidney function is at high risk of kidney injury.
Correct. Prostaglandins protect the stomach lining; blocking them risks a repeat bleed.
Incorrect. Controlled seasonal allergies do not increase NSAID risk.
questions.rationale: Prostaglandins are not only troublemakers; they also protect the stomach lining and maintain kidney blood flow. Blocking them is riskiest for clients with existing kidney impairment (especially older adults) and those with prior GI bleeding. NSAIDs are also a listed trigger for anaphylaxis, so a prior hives-and-wheezing reaction to aspirin is a red flag. The client with seasonal allergies is a tempting choice because allergies sound risky, but controlled rhinitis does not make NSAIDs dangerous.
questions.takeaway: Before an NSAID, screen for kidney impairment, prior GI bleeding, and previous reactions to aspirin or NSAIDs.
questions.hintContent: Think about the protective jobs of prostaglandins and the listed drug triggers of anaphylaxis.
questions.hintStrategy: For each client, link a specific history to a specific consequence of blocking prostaglandins.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old client with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) for 12 years has stable symmetric hand stiffness. Today the client reports that the right knee became hot, red, and very swollen overnight, with shaking chills and a temperature of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F). Which action is the priority?
options: Apply a warm pack to the knee to relieve the RA stiffness
Reassure the client that this is a typical flare of the RA
Encourage gentle range-of-motion exercises of the knee
Notify the provider promptly about a possible new acute process
optionRationales: Incorrect. Warmth is used for chronic stiffness, but it does not address a possible acute infection.
Incorrect. A typical flare does not cause a sudden high fever with rigors in a single joint.
Incorrect. Exercising a hot, acutely inflamed joint can worsen the injury and delays evaluation.
Correct. Sudden fever, rigors, and a single hot joint suggest a new acute process, such as infection, on top of the chronic disease.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation smolders for years with milder local signs, ongoing symptoms, and flares. A sudden high fever with shaking chills and one hot, red, swollen joint has a rapid onset and a different pattern, signaling a new acute process, such as infection, on top of the chronic disease. Calling it a typical flare is the tempting error because the client already has an inflammatory joint disease. Acute, systemic findings in a client with chronic inflammation need prompt reporting.
questions.takeaway: In a client with chronic inflammation, sudden high fever, rigors, or a new hot joint signal a new acute process; report it.
questions.hintContent: Compare today's onset and pattern with the client's long-standing baseline.
questions.hintStrategy: When a chronic client has a sudden change, ask whether it fits the chronic disease or suggests something new and acute.

questions.stem: The nurse in a primary care office is returning four telephone messages. Which client should the nurse call back first?
options: A client with rheumatoid arthritis who reports about 1 hour of morning stiffness, unchanged from usual
A client with COPD who needs a refill of a maintenance inhaler before next week
A client on day 2 of oral antibiotics for cellulitis with chills and redness spreading up the thigh
A client with seasonal allergies who has sneezing, congestion, and itchy eyes again this spring
optionRationales: Incorrect. Morning stiffness at the client's baseline is an expected chronic finding.
Incorrect. A routine refill is important but not urgent.
Correct. Spreading redness and chills despite antibiotics mean the acute inflammation is not resolving and may be becoming systemic.
Incorrect. Seasonal allergy symptoms are a chronic, stable problem.
questions.rationale: Acute inflammation should resolve once the cause is treated, so redness that keeps spreading despite antibiotics is a red flag that the response is not resolving and may be spreading systemically. The chronic conditions described are at baseline or stable. Morning stiffness in RA is tempting because it sounds uncomfortable, but it is unchanged and expected. Acute, worsening, and unstable outranks chronic and stable.
questions.takeaway: Acute inflammation that worsens despite treatment outranks stable chronic symptoms.
questions.hintContent: Which client's problem is changing for the worse right now?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate clients whose findings are described as usual, unchanged, or routine.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old client has had allergic rhinitis with congestion, sneezing, and itchy eyes every spring for 6 years. Symptoms are worse on days with high pollen counts. Which teaching is the nurse's priority to help limit this chronic inflammation?
options: Take the prescribed antihistamine once symptoms begin
Keep windows closed on days when pollen counts are high
Rinse the eyes with cool water whenever they itch
Use a saline nasal spray to clear congestion each day
optionRationales: Incorrect. A prescribed antihistamine eases symptoms, but it treats the response after it starts; avoiding pollen removes the trigger itself.
Correct. Avoiding the trigger stops repeated exposures from restarting the inflammatory response.
Incorrect. Rinsing the eyes is a reasonable comfort measure, but it does nothing to stop repeated pollen exposure from restarting inflammation.
Incorrect. Saline spray can ease congestion, but it relieves one symptom and does not limit exposure to the trigger.
questions.rationale: Allergies are a classic example of chronic inflammation driven by a persistent irritant: every pollen exposure restarts the response before the tissue can recover. The most effective intervention is to avoid or remove the trigger, which is why prevention equals trigger avoidance. The antihistamine option is tempting because it relieves the itching and sneezing, but it treats the response after it starts. Comfort measures such as eye rinses and saline spray help symptoms, but trigger avoidance targets the cause.
questions.takeaway: For chronic inflammation from a recurring trigger, the most effective intervention is avoiding the trigger.
questions.hintContent: Ask what keeps restarting the inflammation each season.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the option that targets the cause of the chronic process rather than a symptom.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old client has long-standing COPD from 45 years of smoking. Refer to the Assessment Findings. Which finding is most important for the home health nurse to report immediately?
options: New confusion with an RR of 32 and an SpO₂ of 84%
A daily cough that produces white sputum each morning
A barrel-shaped chest noted on inspection today
Dyspnea with walking one block at the last clinic visit
optionRationales: Correct. New confusion with worsening oxygenation is an acute change in a chronic disease and signals a threat to breathing.
Incorrect. This is the client's chronic baseline and unchanged from the last visit.
Incorrect. A barrel chest reflects long-term lung changes and is expected in COPD.
Incorrect. Exertional dyspnea 3 months ago was the client's chronic baseline; today's new change is captured by the confusion, RR, and SpO₂.
questions.rationale: COPD is chronic inflammation from years of smoke exposure that slowly damages the airways and air sacs, so a daily cough, a barrel chest, and slowly progressive dyspnea are expected. The nurse's job is to separate this baseline from a new, acute change. Today's confusion, RR of 32, and SpO₂ of 84% are new and threaten oxygenation. The productive cough is tempting because it sounds like infection, but it is unchanged from baseline.
questions.takeaway: In chronic inflammation, compare with baseline: new or acute changes, especially in the ABCs, are what need immediate action.
questions.hintContent: Compare the two columns and find what is new.
questions.hintStrategy: Findings that are unchanged from baseline in a chronic disease are rarely the priority.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old client with rheumatoid arthritis for 9 years reports months of poor appetite, fatigue despite sleeping 8 hours, and an unplanned 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss over 4 months. Vital signs are stable. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Encourage small, frequent meals that are high in calories
Teach the client to weigh daily and report further losses
Complete a nutrition assessment and request a dietitian referral
Encourage short rest periods spaced throughout the day
optionRationales: Incorrect. Small, high-calorie meals may help, but the nurse should assess nutrition first so the plan fits the client's actual intake and needs.
Incorrect. Monitoring weight is useful, but it only tracks the problem; the 6-kg loss already needs assessment and a dietitian.
Correct. Chronic inflammation causes appetite loss and weight loss; nutrition must be assessed and supported to prevent further decline.
Incorrect. Pacing activity with rest helps chronic fatigue, but it does not address the appetite loss and unplanned weight loss.
questions.rationale: Long-standing chronic inflammation keeps mediators circulating for months to years, producing whole-body effects such as fatigue, appetite loss, and unintentional weight loss. These affect healing, activity, and quality of life, so the nurse assesses nutrition and involves the dietitian, a key member of the chronic-care team. Encouraging high-calorie meals is tempting because it targets the weight loss directly, but intervening before assessing risks a plan that misses the real cause. Daily weights and rest periods are useful but address only part of the problem.
questions.takeaway: Fatigue, poor appetite, and weight loss from chronic inflammation need active nutritional assessment and support.
questions.hintContent: Which whole-body effects does long-standing inflammation produce, and who on the team addresses them?
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you act, and choose the option that addresses the actual problem rather than dismissing it.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman has had systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) for 6 years. Refer to the Clinic Data. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider first?
options: The rise in serum creatinine from 0.8 to 2.1 mg/dL
The fatigue that has been present for years
The intermittent aching in the hands and knees
The ESR that remains above the normal range
optionRationales: Correct. A sharply rising creatinine suggests the chronic inflammation is now damaging the kidneys.
Incorrect. Long-standing fatigue is an expected, unchanged effect of chronic inflammation.
Incorrect. Joint aching at the client's baseline is expected in SLE.
Incorrect. A persistently elevated ESR is expected in SLE and has changed little.
questions.rationale: SLE is an autoimmune disease that can cause chronic inflammation in many organs, including the skin, joints, and kidneys, and the ongoing inflammation can damage tissue over time. Fatigue, joint aching, the faint rash, and a mildly elevated ESR are unchanged from baseline. The creatinine has more than doubled, a new sign that the kidneys are being injured. The ESR is the tempting choice because it is abnormal, but it is a stable, nonspecific finding, while the creatinine shows new organ damage.
questions.takeaway: In chronic inflammatory disease, a new sign of organ damage outranks abnormal-but-stable baseline findings.
questions.hintContent: Which organ can SLE inflame, and which result changed the most?
questions.hintStrategy: Abnormal does not equal priority; look for the value that has changed significantly from baseline.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old basketball player is seen in the school clinic 30 minutes after twisting an ankle. The ankle is swollen, warm, and tender. Pedal pulses are strong, the toes are pink and warm, and sensation is intact. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply a warm, moist pack to the ankle
Have the student rest with the ankle up on a pillow
Teach gentle ankle stretches to prevent stiffness
Apply ice wrapped in a cloth and elevate the ankle
optionRationales: Incorrect. Warmth helps stiffness later in healing, but heat early in an acute injury increases blood flow and swelling.
Incorrect. Rest and elevation are part of sprain care, but without ice this is incomplete and does less to limit early swelling.
Incorrect. Stretching helps prevent stiffness during later rehabilitation, but moving a freshly inflamed joint now increases pain and swelling.
Correct. Rest, ice, and elevation limit the swelling of acute inflammation and support healing.
questions.rationale: An ankle sprain is acute inflammation: rapid onset, classic signs, and an expected resolution once the injury heals. Circulation is intact, so the nurse moves to measures that limit swelling and support healing, such as rest, ice, and elevation. Heat is the tempting distractor because warmth soothes chronic stiffness, but in a fresh injury it increases vasodilation and swelling. Exercise is part of later rehabilitation, not the first step.
questions.takeaway: For acute inflammation such as a fresh sprain, the goal is to limit swelling and support healing with rest, ice, and elevation.
questions.hintContent: Is this injury acute or chronic, and what is the nursing goal for that type?
questions.hintStrategy: Once the stem rules out circulatory compromise, choose the intervention that matches the stage of inflammation.
