questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 44-year-old client whose mother has rheumatoid arthritis asks what she can do to lower her own risk of a chronic inflammatory disease. She smokes a pack of cigarettes per day, walks most days, and eats mostly home-cooked meals. Which teaching is the priority?
options: Arrange genetic testing for RA risk
Support her in quitting smoking
Encourage her to keep walking daily
Add more fish and vegetables to meals
optionRationales: Incorrect. Testing may answer her questions about inheritance, but genetics is a nonmodifiable risk; results do not lower her risk.
Correct. Smoking is a modifiable risk factor and a persistent irritant that drives chronic inflammation.
Incorrect. Regular walking lowers inflammation and should continue, but she already does it, so it adds less benefit than quitting smoking.
Incorrect. An anti-inflammatory diet helps, but she already eats mostly home-cooked meals; daily smoking is the larger risk she can change.
questions.rationale: Family history, genetics, and age are nonmodifiable risk factors, so the nurse focuses on what the client can change: not smoking, a healthy weight, regular exercise, and a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, fish, and whole grains. This client already walks and eats home-cooked meals, but she smokes daily, so smoking cessation offers the greatest benefit. Genetic testing is tempting because her mother's RA raises the question of inheritance, but knowing her loci does not lower her risk. The priority is the risk she can modify.
questions.takeaway: When family history raises risk, teach the client to change the modifiable risk factors, starting with the biggest one present.
questions.hintContent: Separate the risk factors she can change from those she cannot.
questions.hintStrategy: Look in the stem for the one unhealthy behavior the client actually has; the priority teaching targets it.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with long-standing COPD is admitted with right upper quadrant pain that began 8 hours ago after a fatty meal. Findings: T 38.7 °C (101.7 °F), HR 104/min, WBC 15,800/mm³ with 11% bands, and a chronic cough at baseline. Which problem should the nurse address as the priority?
options: Chronic airway inflammation from many years of cigarette smoking
Acute gallbladder inflammation needing treatment of the cause
Fatigue related to long-standing chronic inflammation
Risk for weight loss related to chronic lung disease
optionRationales: Incorrect. The COPD is at baseline and is not the cause of today's acute findings.
Correct. Rapid onset, fever, and a neutrophil response with bands point to an acute process that needs treatment now.
Incorrect. Fatigue is a chronic concern and is lower priority than an acute, systemic process.
Incorrect. This is a long-term risk, not an immediate threat.
questions.rationale: Acute inflammation has a rapid onset, classic and systemic signs, and a neutrophil-driven response with increased bands. Acute cholecystitis is an example that may require hospitalization and surgery, and here the fever, tachycardia, and left shift show the response is becoming systemic. The COPD is tempting because it is a serious disease, but it is at baseline and stable. Acute and unstable takes priority over chronic and stable.
questions.takeaway: When acute inflammation appears on top of a stable chronic disease, the acute process is the priority.
questions.hintContent: Which process started hours ago, and which has been present for years?
questions.hintStrategy: Prioritize the problem that is new, systemic, and potentially unstable.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a 19-year-old client admitted with acute appendicitis who is scheduled for an appendectomy. Which nursing goal is the priority?
options: Relieve the abdominal pain so the client can rest
Teach deep breathing and coughing for after surgery
Create a long-term plan to prevent future flares
Remove the cause and monitor for spreading inflammation
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pain relief is an important comfort goal, but it does not address the safety risk of rupture and spreading inflammation.
Incorrect. Postoperative breathing teaching is appropriate, but it is a later goal and lower priority than treating the inflamed appendix.
Incorrect. Long-term flare prevention is a goal for chronic inflammation, not for acute appendicitis that resolves once removed.
Correct. The goal for acute inflammation is to treat or remove the cause and watch for spread or systemic signs.
questions.rationale: Acute and chronic inflammation call for different nursing goals. For acute inflammation, the goal is to remove or treat the cause and support healing, so the appendicitis is treated surgically while the nurse monitors for spread, rupture, and systemic signs. Chronic inflammation calls for long-term control and self-management, including trigger avoidance, medications, diet, activity, and flare recognition. Pain relief and postoperative teaching are tempting because they are real needs, but they rank below removing the cause and watching for rupture.
questions.takeaway: Acute inflammation: remove the cause and monitor for spread. Chronic inflammation: long-term control and self-management.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether appendicitis is acute or chronic, then recall the goal for that type.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the goal to the type of inflammation; eliminate options that belong to the other type.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is recovering after an appendectomy for acute appendicitis. His wife has had systemic lupus erythematosus for 10 years. He asks, “Will I need medicine for the rest of my life like she does?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Yours was acute, so removing the cause should end it; her lupus is chronic.”
“Yes, any inflammation tends to come back and needs lifelong treatment.”
“Appendicitis often turns into lupus, so you'll need regular blood tests.”
“You'll need long-term medicine only if your inflammation markers stay high.”
optionRationales: Correct. Acute inflammation resolves once the cause is removed; SLE is chronic and needs long-term control.
Incorrect. Acute inflammation resolves once the cause is neutralized; it does not require lifelong treatment.
Incorrect. Appendicitis does not become lupus; SLE is an autoimmune process.
Incorrect. This implies an acute surgical problem becomes a chronic disease, which is inaccurate.
questions.rationale: Acute inflammation starts quickly, shows the classic signs, and resolves once the cause is neutralized; removing the inflamed appendix removed the cause. Chronic inflammation, such as SLE, lasts months to years, often arises independently, and needs long-term control and self-management. The lifelong-treatment option is tempting because the client sees his wife's experience, but the two types of inflammation behave very differently. Explaining the difference addresses his concern accurately.
questions.takeaway: Acute inflammation resolves once its cause is removed; chronic inflammation needs long-term management.
questions.hintContent: Compare how acute and chronic inflammation end.
questions.hintStrategy: In 'best response' items, choose the option that is accurate and directly answers the client's concern.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse reviews self-management with a 58-year-old client who has had rheumatoid arthritis for 7 years. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I'll keep taking my medicine even on days when I feel good.”
“I'll call the clinic early if my joints start getting hotter and stiffer.”
“Once this flare settles down, my arthritis will be cured.”
“Staying active and doing my physical therapy helps my mobility.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is accurate; adherence supports long-term control of chronic inflammation.
Incorrect. This is accurate; recognizing flares early is part of self-management.
Correct. This needs correcting: RA is chronic inflammation that flares and settles over years; a flare ending is not a cure.
Incorrect. This is accurate; activity and physical therapy restore strength and mobility.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation lasts months to years, with symptoms that persist and flare over time rather than resolving. Self-management includes taking medications as prescribed, staying active, eating an anti-inflammatory diet, and recognizing flares early. The belief that a flare ending equals a cure confuses chronic with acute inflammation, which does resolve once the cause is removed. That misunderstanding could lead the client to stop treatment.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation is controlled, not cured; the end of a flare is not the end of the disease.
questions.hintContent: Recall how chronic inflammation behaves over many years.
questions.hintStrategy: In 'further teaching' items, find the statement that is inaccurate; the accurate statements are distractors.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A synovial tissue biopsy from a 55-year-old client with long-standing joint swelling shows large numbers of lymphocytes and macrophages, along with fibrous scar tissue. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: Acute inflammation that should resolve once the cause is removed
Normal tissue repair, since scar tissue is replacing damaged tissue
Chronic infection that needs a long course of antibiotics
Chronic inflammation causing ongoing tissue damage
optionRationales: Incorrect. Inflammation is present, but acute inflammation is led by neutrophils and resolves; lymphocytes, macrophages, and scarring point to a long-standing process.
Incorrect. Scar tissue is part of repair, but the ongoing lymphocyte and macrophage infiltrate shows the injury is continuing, not finished.
Incorrect. The process is chronic, but these cells and scarring describe chronic inflammation, such as in RA, which is not caused by infection or cured by antibiotics.
Correct. Lymphocytes and macrophages dominate chronic inflammation, and fibrous scarring reflects repeated tissue injury that is still occurring.
questions.rationale: In acute inflammation, fast, short-lived neutrophils lead the response, and the tissue heals. In chronic inflammation, lymphocytes and macrophages dominate and keep releasing mediators instead of finishing the job, so the tissue is damaged and repaired with fibrous scar, gradually losing normal structure. The normal-repair option is tempting because scar tissue is part of healing, but the persistent lymphocytes and macrophages show the injury is ongoing. This pattern explains joint deformity in long-standing RA.
questions.takeaway: Neutrophils mean acute inflammation; lymphocytes, macrophages, and scarring mean chronic inflammation.
questions.hintContent: Which white cells lead each type of inflammation?
questions.hintStrategy: Use the cell type in the data as the deciding cue between acute and chronic.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 31-year-old client newly diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus says, “I never had an injury or an infection, so how can I have chronic inflammation?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Chronic inflammation can follow an acute injury or infection that never healed.”
“Lupus is lifelong, but treatment can help keep your symptoms under control.”
“Chronic inflammation often starts on its own, as when the immune system attacks tissue.”
“It's normal to feel confused by a new diagnosis. Tell me more about your worry.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only one route and does not explain how the client developed chronic inflammation without an injury.
Incorrect. This is accurate and hopeful, but it does not answer the client's question about how the inflammation began.
Correct. Chronic inflammation may follow acute inflammation but often develops independently, as when the immune system attacks the body's own tissue in lupus.
Incorrect. Acknowledging feelings is therapeutic, but the client asked a direct question, and the best response gives accurate information.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation may follow an acute episode, but it often develops independently. In autoimmune disease such as SLE, the immune system targets the body's own tissue, so the response can never finish its job and continues for years. The 'follows an acute injury' option is tempting because it is true, but it does not explain this client's case. Correcting this helps the client understand why long-term self-management is needed.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation does not need a prior acute episode; it often develops independently, as in autoimmune disease.
questions.hintContent: Watch the wording 'often develops independently.'
questions.hintStrategy: Be wary of options that use 'always' or assume a hidden cause the stem does not support.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 26-year-old client with Crohn's disease asks, “Is my kind of illness rare? I don't know anyone else who has one.” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “They are very rare and affect fewer than 1 in every 10,000 people worldwide.”
“They're common; together they affect about 5% to 7% of people in Western countries.”
“They are extremely common and affect about half of all adults by middle age.”
“No one tracks them, so there is no way to know how common they really are.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This greatly underestimates how common chronic inflammatory diseases are.
Correct. About 100 chronic inflammatory diseases have been identified, and 5–7% of the Western population has at least one.
Incorrect. This greatly overestimates the prevalence of chronic inflammatory disease.
Incorrect. Chronic inflammatory diseases are tracked; about 100 have been identified. It is acute inflammation whose prevalence is unknown, because it is so common.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammatory diseases are a major global health threat; about 100 have been identified, and 5–7% of the Western population is affected by at least one. The World Health Organization ranks chronic disease as the greatest threat to human health. The 'no one knows' option is tempting because it describes acute inflammation, whose prevalence is unknown because nearly everyone experiences it. Accurate information can reduce the client's sense of isolation.
questions.takeaway: About 100 chronic inflammatory diseases affect 5–7% of people in Western countries; acute inflammation is too common to count.
questions.hintContent: Recall which type of inflammation has an unknown prevalence and why.
questions.hintStrategy: When two answers sound plausible, check whether one applies to the other type of inflammation.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 38-year-old client with psoriasis says, “My brother has Crohn's disease. If inflammation runs in our family, why don't we have the same disease?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Each disease has its own genetic profile, though many share a common immune pathway.”
“Genes are only part of it; smoking and diet also affect your risk of disease.”
“They share one immune pathway, so they are really the same disease in two places.”
“You and your brother share many genes, so your two diseases are closely related.”
optionRationales: Correct. Each disease has a unique genetic profile, while many share the IL-23/IL-17 cytokine pathway, which explains both the family link and the different diseases.
Incorrect. Modifiable factors do matter, but this does not explain why siblings with a family tendency developed different diseases.
Incorrect. Many of these diseases do share the IL-23/IL-17 pathway, but each has its own genetic profile and is a distinct disease.
Incorrect. Shared genes help explain the family clustering, but this does not explain why each sibling developed a different disease.
questions.rationale: About 450 genetic loci have been linked to inflammation, and each inflammatory disease has its own unique genetic profile, so the pattern in psoriasis differs from that in Crohn's disease. Many of these diseases still share a common pathway, IL-23/IL-17 cytokine regulation, which helps explain why they cluster in families. The shared-pathway option is tempting because the pathway is real, but sharing a pathway does not make them the same disease. The nurse can also encourage the risk factors the client can change.
questions.takeaway: Inflammatory diseases have distinct genetic profiles but often share the IL-23/IL-17 pathway; family history is a nonmodifiable risk.
questions.hintContent: Recall what is unique and what is shared in the genetics of inflammatory disease.
questions.hintStrategy: Reject absolute answers (no link at all, or one gene causes all) when the science is more nuanced.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is caring for a 58-year-old client admitted with acute cellulitis of the lower leg who is receiving IV antibiotics. Which task can the RN delegate to the UAP?
options: Check whether the redness has spread past the marked border
Teach the client which signs of worsening infection to report
Keep the affected leg elevated on pillows as instructed
Evaluate whether the client is responding to the antibiotics
optionRationales: Incorrect. Assessing the spread of inflammation is an RN responsibility.
Incorrect. Client teaching is an RN responsibility.
Correct. Positioning a stable client as directed is within the UAP's scope and supports healing.
Incorrect. Evaluating response to treatment requires RN judgment.
questions.rationale: Care for acute inflammation such as cellulitis includes treating the cause, elevating the limb, and monitoring for spread or systemic signs. The UAP can perform routine care for a stable client, such as positioning the leg as directed. Checking the marked border is tempting because it seems like simple observation, but judging whether inflammation is spreading is assessment. Teaching and evaluation also remain with the RN.
questions.takeaway: UAP can position and assist; assessing spread, teaching, and evaluating response stay with the RN.
questions.hintContent: Which tasks require judgment about whether the inflammation is getting better or worse?
questions.hintStrategy: For delegation, eliminate any option containing assess, teach, or evaluate.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 69-year-old client has had COPD for 15 years. Which finding should the nurse expect as a reflection of the chronic inflammatory process?
options: Shortness of breath that has slowly worsened over years
A fever with yellow sputum that began two days ago
A CBC showing a sharp rise in neutrophils with 15% bands
Chest tightness that eased fully after one inhaler dose
optionRationales: Correct. Chronic inflammation causes slow, progressive tissue damage that steadily limits airflow over years.
Incorrect. Clients with COPD do have flares, but a new fever with purulent sputum signals an acute infection, not the chronic process.
Incorrect. This is an inflammatory finding, but a neutrophil and band rise (left shift) reflects an acute process.
Incorrect. Airway tightness occurs in COPD, but symptoms that fully reverse quickly suggest acute bronchospasm, not progressive chronic damage.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation lasts months to years and is driven by lymphocytes and macrophages that keep injuring tissue, so organ function declines gradually. In COPD, years of airway inflammation from smoke slowly narrow the airways and damage the air sacs, causing dyspnea that progresses over years. The left-shift option is tempting because it is an inflammatory lab finding, but a neutrophil and band response signals an acute process. A new fever with sputum and fully reversible tightness also fit acute problems.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation produces gradual, progressive damage; sudden fever, bands, or quick resolution point to an acute process.
questions.hintContent: Think about the time course of chronic inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each option into acute or chronic by its onset, duration, and cell type.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A 64-year-old client with rheumatoid arthritis for 20 years reports that joint stiffness and weakness now make it hard to climb stairs and to walk to the mailbox. Which referral is most appropriate?
options: Registered dietitian
Home health aide
Medical social worker
Physical therapist
optionRationales: Incorrect. The dietitian is part of the chronic-inflammation team, but the client's stated problem is mobility, not nutrition.
Incorrect. An aide can help with daily tasks, but cannot evaluate or rebuild the strength and joint mobility the client has lost.
Incorrect. A social worker can arrange resources and support, but does not treat the stiffness and weakness limiting mobility.
Correct. Physical therapy restores strength and mobility, which directly addresses the client's trouble with stairs and walking.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation slowly damages tissue, and in RA the result can be joint deformity, stiffness, and weakness that limit daily activities. The collaborative team for chronic inflammation often includes a dietitian and a physical therapist; the PT restores strength and mobility. The dietitian is tempting because the dietitian is also part of the chronic-care team, but the client's problem is mobility rather than nutrition. Matching the referral to the stated problem is the key.
questions.takeaway: In chronic inflammation, refer to physical therapy when the problem is strength and mobility, and to a dietitian when it is nutrition.
questions.hintContent: Which team member restores strength and mobility?
questions.hintStrategy: Match the referral to the specific problem described in the stem.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 50-year-old client with Crohn's disease about an anti-inflammatory eating pattern. Which lunch choice by the client indicates that the teaching was understood?
options: A turkey sandwich on white bread with baked chips
Grilled salmon with brown rice and roasted vegetables
A fruit smoothie made with juice and added honey
A veggie pizza on a white crust with a diet soda
optionRationales: Incorrect. Lean turkey and baked chips seem healthy, but processed deli meat and refined white bread do not fit an anti-inflammatory pattern.
Correct. Fish, whole grains, and vegetables are the foundation of an anti-inflammatory diet.
Incorrect. Fruit fits the pattern, but juice and added honey make this high in sugar, which promotes inflammation.
Incorrect. The vegetables fit, but the refined white crust and processed soda reflect the Western pattern that promotes inflammation.
questions.rationale: Long-term self-management of chronic inflammation includes an anti-inflammatory diet rich in fruits, vegetables, fish, and whole grains. The Western diet, with fast food, sugar, refined grains, and little fiber, promotes inflammation. The turkey sandwich is the tempting distractor because it seems like a healthy choice, but refined grains and processed meat do not fit the pattern. Choosing salmon, whole grains, and vegetables shows understanding. Clients with Crohn's disease may also have individual food triggers to avoid, which the dietitian helps identify.
questions.takeaway: An anti-inflammatory diet emphasizes fruits, vegetables, fish, and whole grains and limits fast food and sugar.
questions.hintContent: Picture the foods that lower inflammation versus those in a typical Western diet.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each meal against the teaching; only one option fits every element.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 45-year-old client is admitted with acute cholecystitis. Which findings are consistent with an acute inflammatory process? Select all that apply.
options: Fatigue and a 7-kg weight loss over 8 months
WBC 15,000/mm³ with 9% bands
A biopsy showing mainly lymphocytes and macrophages
Right upper quadrant pain that began 6 hours ago
Tenderness and guarding over the gallbladder
optionRationales: Incorrect. Months of fatigue and weight loss reflect chronic inflammation.
Correct. An acute response is neutrophil-driven, with increased bands.
Incorrect. Lymphocytes and macrophages dominate chronic inflammation.
Correct. Acute inflammation has a rapid onset, over minutes to hours.
Correct. Pain and impaired function are classic signs of acute inflammation.
questions.rationale: Acute inflammation develops over minutes to hours, shows classic signs such as pain, tenderness, and impaired function, and is led by neutrophils, often with increased bands. Acute cholecystitis is an example that may need hospitalization or surgery. Fatigue and weight loss over months and a lymphocyte- and macrophage-rich biopsy are tempting because they are inflammatory findings, but they point to a chronic process. Sorting findings by onset and cell type separates the two types.
questions.takeaway: Acute: hours, classic signs, neutrophils and bands. Chronic: months, fatigue and weight loss, lymphocytes and macrophages.
questions.hintContent: Use timing and cell type to sort each finding.
questions.hintStrategy: Mark each option acute or chronic, then select only the acute ones.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the day's schedule in an internal medicine clinic. Which clients have a chronic inflammatory condition? Select all that apply.
options: A 42-year-old with systemic lupus erythematosus
A 68-year-old with COPD from long-term smoking
A 55-year-old with cellulitis that began 2 days ago
A 30-year-old with a wrist sprain from yesterday
A 19-year-old with a sunburn from the weekend
A 23-year-old with allergies that recur every spring and fall
optionRationales: Correct. SLE is an autoimmune disease that produces chronic inflammation.
Correct. COPD is years of airway inflammation, a chronic process.
Incorrect. Cellulitis is acute inflammation that resolves with antibiotics.
Incorrect. A fresh sprain is acute inflammation that resolves as the injury heals.
Incorrect. A sunburn is acute inflammation that resolves on its own.
Correct. Repeated allergic inflammation is an example of chronic inflammation.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation lasts months to years and includes allergies, COPD, and autoimmune diseases such as SLE and RA. Acute inflammation, such as a sprain, sunburn, or cellulitis, develops quickly and resolves once the cause is neutralized. Allergies are the most commonly missed chronic example because each individual reaction seems brief, but repeated exposure keeps restarting the response. Recognizing the type guides the nursing goal: healing for acute, long-term self-management for chronic.
questions.takeaway: Chronic examples: allergies, COPD, SLE, RA. Acute examples: sprain, sunburn, cellulitis, appendicitis.
questions.hintContent: Consider the time course of each condition, not how severe it sounds.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify each client by duration; recurring conditions over years are chronic.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 37-year-old client has had Crohn's disease for 5 years. Which self-management points should the nurse include in the teaching plan? Select all that apply.
options: Stop medications once a flare has fully settled
Learn the early signs of a flare and report them promptly
Expect the disease to resolve completely within a few months
Identify and avoid personal food triggers
Take prescribed medications even when symptoms are quiet
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stopping treatment when well allows the chronic process to flare again.
Correct. Recognizing flares early is a core self-management skill.
Incorrect. Chronic inflammation lasts years; it is controlled, not cured, by treatment.
Correct. Avoiding triggers limits repeated restarts of the inflammatory response.
Correct. Adherence supports long-term control of chronic inflammation.
questions.rationale: The goal for chronic inflammation is long-term control and self-management: avoiding triggers, taking medications as prescribed, following an anti-inflammatory diet, staying active, and recognizing flares early. Stopping medications after a flare is tempting because the client feels well, but the underlying process continues. Expecting complete resolution confuses chronic with acute inflammation. Teaching realistic expectations improves adherence.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation care is long-term self-management: medications, trigger avoidance, and early flare recognition.
questions.hintContent: Recall the nursing goal for chronic inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Reject options that treat a chronic disease as if it will end once symptoms improve.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: During a health history, a 68-year-old client asks about personal risk for chronic inflammatory disease. Which findings are nonmodifiable risk factors? Select all that apply.
options: Eats fast food most days
Body mass index of 34
Smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day
Mother had rheumatoid arthritis
Sister has systemic lupus erythematosus
Age 68 years
optionRationales: Incorrect. Diet is modifiable; a Western diet promotes inflammation.
Incorrect. Obesity is linked to chronic inflammation but can be modified.
Incorrect. Smoking is a modifiable risk factor.
Correct. Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor.
Correct. A first-degree relative with an autoimmune disease is part of family history, which cannot be changed.
Correct. Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor; older adults tend to have higher baseline inflammation.
questions.rationale: Nonmodifiable risk factors are those the client cannot change: genetics, age, and family history. A mother with RA and a sister with SLE are both family history, and age 68 adds to baseline inflammation. Smoking, obesity, and diet are modifiable; obesity is the tempting choice because it is linked to chronic inflammation, but weight can change. Identifying nonmodifiable risks tells the nurse whom to watch closely and who benefits most from changing the modifiable ones.
questions.takeaway: Nonmodifiable: genetics, age, family history. Modifiable: smoking, weight, diet, and activity.
questions.hintContent: Ask of each factor: can the client change it?
questions.hintStrategy: Separate 'linked to inflammation' from 'cannot be changed'; the question asks for the second.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 21-year-old client has an acute knee sprain from a fall 2 hours ago. Which interventions fit the nursing goal for acute inflammation? Select all that apply.
options: Rest the knee and limit weight bearing
Elevate the leg above heart level
Develop a long-term plan to avoid flare triggers
Apply ice wrapped in a towel
Begin vigorous range-of-motion exercises today
optionRationales: Correct. Rest protects the injured tissue and supports healing.
Correct. Elevation reduces swelling.
Incorrect. Trigger avoidance is a chronic-care goal; a sprain resolves as it heals.
Correct. Ice limits swelling and eases pain early in acute inflammation.
Incorrect. Vigorous exercise of a fresh sprain increases pain and swelling.
questions.rationale: The goal for acute inflammation is to remove or treat the cause and support healing, using rest, ice, elevation, positioning, pain control, and monitoring for spread. A sprain is acute inflammation that resolves as the injury heals. A trigger-avoidance plan is tempting because it sounds preventive, but it belongs to chronic inflammation care. Vigorous exercise belongs to later rehabilitation, not the first hours.
questions.takeaway: Acute inflammation care: rest, ice, elevation, and pain control to support healing.
questions.hintContent: Recall the nursing goal for acute inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Select interventions that match acute care, and reject those designed for chronic, long-term management.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 60-year-old client with rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years is seen in the clinic. Which findings suggest a new acute process on top of the chronic inflammation and should be reported promptly? Select all that apply.
options: Symmetric swelling of the finger joints, unchanged
WBC 16,200/mm³ with 14% bands
Redness spreading rapidly over the left calf
Morning stiffness lasting about an hour, as usual
Temperature of 39.1 °C (102.4 °F) with shaking chills since this morning
Fatigue that has persisted for years
optionRationales: Incorrect. Unchanged symmetric joint swelling is the client's chronic baseline.
Correct. A neutrophil response with bands signals an acute bacterial process.
Correct. Rapidly spreading redness suggests acute infection, such as cellulitis.
Incorrect. Morning stiffness at baseline is expected in long-standing RA.
Correct. A sudden high fever with rigors suggests a new acute process, such as infection.
Incorrect. Long-standing fatigue is an expected effect of chronic inflammation.
questions.rationale: A client with chronic inflammation can develop a new acute process, such as infection, on top of the chronic disease. Clues are a rapid onset, a sudden high fever or rigors, rapidly spreading redness, and a neutrophil response with increased bands. Findings that are unchanged and long-standing, such as morning stiffness and fatigue, are the client's baseline. Fatigue is tempting because it is a real problem, but it does not signal a new acute threat.
questions.takeaway: In chronic inflammation, new rapid-onset fever, rigors, spreading redness, or bands signal an acute process to report.
questions.hintContent: Compare each finding with what has been present for years.
questions.hintStrategy: Words like 'as usual,' 'unchanged,' and 'for years' mark baseline findings.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 62-year-old client with COPD and a 40 pack-year history about why the lung inflammation persists. Which client statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “Quitting smoking is the best way to slow the damage.”
“Since my COPD started slowly, smoking now doesn't make a difference.”
“Every cigarette I smoke restarts the inflammation in my lungs.”
“After this round of antibiotics, my lungs will heal completely.”
“Antibiotics treat infections on top of my COPD but don't stop the COPD itself.”
optionRationales: Correct. Removing the trigger is the most effective intervention for chronic inflammation from an irritant.
Incorrect. Ongoing smoking continues to drive the chronic inflammation.
Correct. Daily smoke exposure is a persistent irritant that keeps the chronic response going.
Incorrect. COPD involves ongoing tissue damage; antibiotics do not reverse chronic inflammation.
Correct. Antibiotics treat acute infections but do not stop the chronic process.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation persists when its cause never goes away. In COPD, cigarette smoke is inhaled every day, restarting the response before the tissue can recover, so the most effective intervention is smoking cessation. Antibiotics treat acute infections on top of COPD but do not stop the chronic process. Believing the lungs will heal completely after antibiotics is tempting, but it confuses chronic tissue damage with acute inflammation that resolves.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation from a persistent irritant continues until the irritant is removed; antibiotics do not stop it.
questions.hintContent: What keeps restarting the inflammation in COPD?
questions.hintStrategy: Select statements that link the persistent cause to the chronic process; reject those that expect a cure.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 57-year-old client with rheumatoid arthritis for 18 years asks why her fingers have become permanently bent. Which explanations by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: “A bacterial infection inside the joints has slowly bent your fingers.”
“Neutrophils clear the inflammation in a few days, but the swelling stays.”
“Lymphocytes and macrophages keep releasing chemicals that inflame the joints.”
“The body repairs the damage with scar tissue that changes the joint's shape.”
“The constant inflammation damages the joint tissue itself.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. RA is an autoimmune process, not a bacterial infection.
Incorrect. Neutrophils lead acute, not chronic, inflammation.
Correct. These cells dominate chronic inflammation and keep the response going.
Correct. Fibrous repair gradually alters the joint's structure and function.
Correct. Chronic inflammation causes ongoing tissue damage rather than healing.
questions.rationale: In chronic inflammation, lymphocytes and macrophages keep releasing mediators instead of finishing the job, so constant inflammation damages the tissue. The body repairs it with fibrous scar, and the joint gradually loses its normal structure, which is how RA produces deformity. The neutrophil option is tempting because neutrophils are the best-known inflammatory cells, but they lead short-lived acute inflammation. RA is autoimmune, so infection does not explain the deformity.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation deforms tissue through ongoing lymphocyte and macrophage activity and scar repair.
questions.hintContent: Recall the cells and outcome of chronic inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each explanation for the right cell type and the right type of inflammation.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: An urgent care nurse is triaging five clients who each have acute inflammation. Which clients most likely need transfer for hospital care rather than self-care at home? Select all that apply.
options: A 49-year-old with right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal, fever, and 10% bands
A 54-year-old with leg cellulitis spreading over 6 hours, T 38.9 °C (102 °F), and HR 108/min
A 26-year-old with a mild sunburn on the shoulders and normal vital signs
A 33-year-old with a mild ankle sprain who can bear weight and has normal pulses
A 20-year-old with right lower quadrant pain, rebound tenderness, and WBC 15,400/mm³
optionRationales: Correct. These findings suggest acute cholecystitis, which may require hospitalization and surgery.
Correct. Rapidly spreading cellulitis with systemic signs often needs IV antibiotics in the hospital.
Incorrect. A mild sunburn is acute inflammation that resolves on its own.
Incorrect. A mild sprain usually resolves with rest, ice, and elevation at home.
Correct. These findings suggest appendicitis, which requires surgery.
questions.rationale: Acute inflammation may resolve on its own, as with a minor sprain or sunburn, or it may require hospitalization, as with cellulitis needing IV antibiotics or appendicitis and cholecystitis needing surgery. Systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, a rising WBC or bands) and organ involvement signal the need for a higher level of care. The sprain is a tempting choice because the client is in pain, but normal pulses and weight bearing indicate a self-limiting injury. Recognizing which acute processes will not resolve on their own guides triage.
questions.takeaway: Acute inflammation with systemic signs or an inflamed organ needing surgery requires hospital care; minor sprains and sunburns resolve at home.
questions.hintContent: Which acute conditions resolve on their own, and which need antibiotics or surgery?
questions.hintStrategy: Look for systemic signs or organ involvement as the cue that a higher level of care is needed.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 45-year-old client received epinephrine 0.5 mg IM 10 minutes ago for anaphylaxis after the first dose of IV ceftriaxone, and the infusion was stopped. The client still has audible wheezing and throat tightness; BP is 82/48 mm Hg and SpO₂ is 90% on high-flow oxygen. The protocol allows repeat epinephrine every 5–15 minutes. Which action is the priority now?
options: Give IV diphenhydramine and reassess in 30 minutes
Give a repeat dose of epinephrine IM as prescribed
Give an albuterol nebulizer to relieve the wheezing
Notify the provider before giving more epinephrine
optionRationales: Incorrect. Antihistamines are useful adjuncts, but they do not reverse airway swelling or hypotension, and waiting 30 minutes delays the drug that does.
Correct. Symptoms continue 10 minutes after the first dose, so a repeat dose is indicated within the 5–15 minute window.
Incorrect. Albuterol can ease bronchospasm, but it does not treat throat swelling or hypotension, so epinephrine comes first.
Incorrect. The provider should be updated, but the protocol already allows a repeat dose, and waiting for a call delays treatment.
questions.rationale: After epinephrine, the response is judged mainly by blood pressure and breathing. Persistent wheezing, throat tightness, hypotension, and low SpO₂ 10 minutes after the first dose mean the reaction is not controlled, so a repeat dose is given within the 5–15 minute window. Calling the provider first is tempting because the first dose did not work, but deaths occur most often when epinephrine is given too late. Antihistamines, bronchodilators, and steroids remain second-line adjuncts.
questions.takeaway: If anaphylaxis symptoms continue 5–15 minutes after epinephrine, repeat the epinephrine; do not wait or substitute.
questions.hintContent: Check how long it has been since the first dose and what the protocol allows.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate the response by BP and breathing; if they have not improved, repeat the first-line action.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 33-year-old client was treated in the emergency department for anaphylaxis after eating cashews. Two hours after one dose of IM epinephrine, the client has no symptoms and says, “I feel fine now, so I'd like to go home.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “You can go home now because the epinephrine has fully reversed the reaction.”
“You can go home if you take an antihistamine every 4 hours through the night.”
“Before you leave, let me show you how to use an epinephrine auto-injector.”
“Symptoms can return hours later even without more nuts, so you need to stay longer.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The client is symptom-free now, but epinephrine wears off, and a second-wave reaction can occur hours later.
Incorrect. Antihistamines are often prescribed afterward, but they do not prevent a biphasic reaction and do not replace observation.
Incorrect. Auto-injector teaching is essential before discharge, but 2 hours is too early to discharge after anaphylaxis.
Correct. A biphasic reaction can occur hours later without re-exposure, so a longer observation period is needed.
questions.rationale: After anaphylaxis, symptoms can return hours later in a second-wave (biphasic) reaction, even without a new exposure, so clients are usually observed for at least 4–6 hours, longer after a severe reaction. Two hours is not long enough. Discharging with an antihistamine is tempting because it sounds protective, but antihistamines do not stop a biphasic reaction. The nurse explains the risk so the client can make an informed decision, respecting autonomy.
questions.takeaway: After anaphylaxis, observe for several hours because a biphasic reaction can occur without re-exposure.
questions.hintContent: Think about what can happen after the first wave of anaphylaxis resolves.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the response that gives accurate information about the risk while respecting the client's autonomy.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client is being treated for anaphylaxis after a shellfish exposure. After IM epinephrine, BP is 128/78 mm Hg and HR is 104/min, but the client still has wheezing and says, “I can't get enough air lying flat.” Which position is best for this client now?
options: Help the client sit upright
Keep the client flat with the legs elevated
Place the client in a side-lying position
Place the client in a low semi-Fowler's position
optionRationales: Correct. When breathing is the main problem and BP is stable, sitting fully upright best eases the work of breathing.
Incorrect. This is the position for hypotension in anaphylaxis, but the BP is stable here, and lying flat worsens the breathing problem.
Incorrect. Side-lying protects the airway if the client vomits or is drowsy, but it does not ease this alert client's breathing.
Incorrect. Raising the head helps somewhat, but a low angle gives less lung expansion than sitting fully upright.
questions.rationale: Positioning in anaphylaxis depends on which problem dominates. If the BP is low, the client lies flat with the legs raised to support circulation. If breathing is the main problem and the BP is stable, the client sits up to ease breathing. Keeping the client flat with the legs up is the tempting answer because it is the best-known anaphylaxis position, but here it would worsen the breathing problem. A partly raised head is better than flat but less effective than sitting upright.
questions.takeaway: In anaphylaxis: low BP, lie flat with legs raised; breathing problem with stable BP, sit up; never stand or walk.
questions.hintContent: Is this client's main problem circulation or breathing?
questions.hintStrategy: Let the data in the stem (BP stable, dyspnea lying flat) choose the position rather than a memorized default.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A 40-year-old client with a documented latex allergy, whose past reaction included lip swelling and hives, is on a surgical unit. The nurse sees the UAP preparing to give perineal care wearing latex gloves taken from an old supply box. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Remind the UAP about the client's documented latex allergy
Check that the client is wearing a latex allergy wristband
Stop the UAP and provide latex-free gloves before care begins
Report the old latex glove supply to the charge nurse today
optionRationales: Incorrect. A reminder is reasonable, but it does not guarantee the gloves are changed; the nurse must stop the care and supply latex-free gloves.
Incorrect. Allergy identification matters, but the allergy is already documented, and checking does not stop the exposure about to happen.
Correct. Preventing contact with the trigger is the first step; stopping care and supplying latex-free gloves removes the exposure.
Incorrect. Removing latex supplies is an important follow-up, but it comes after the immediate exposure is prevented.
questions.rationale: Latex is a listed anaphylaxis trigger, and this client's past lip swelling shows the reaction was more than a mild rash. Prevention depends on avoiding the trigger, so latex-free equipment must be used for every contact. Reminding the UAP is tempting because it addresses the error, but the nurse must ensure the exposure does not happen. The nurse intervenes before care begins, then reports the supply problem and reinforces the latex-safe environment with the team.
questions.takeaway: For a client with a latex allergy, prevent contact first; use latex-free equipment for every task.
questions.hintContent: Which action keeps the trigger from reaching the client at all?
questions.hintStrategy: Safety items: prevention of harm comes before monitoring or documentation.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 58-year-old client is 4 hours post-op after a hernia repair. The allergy list states “ibuprofen: throat swelling and hives.” A new prescription reads ketorolac 15 mg IV every 6 hours for pain. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Ask the client to describe the past reaction to ibuprofen first
Give acetaminophen for the pain instead and document the reason
Ask the pharmacist to verify that the ketorolac dose is correct
Hold the ketorolac and contact the prescriber about the NSAID allergy
optionRationales: Incorrect. Clarifying a reaction is good practice, but throat swelling is already documented, so the risk is clear and the drug must be held.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen may be a safe choice, but substituting a drug without a prescription is outside the nurse's scope.
Incorrect. Involving the pharmacist is reasonable, but the dose is not the problem; the drug class is, and the prescriber must change the order.
Correct. Ketorolac is an NSAID like ibuprofen, so the nurse holds it and contacts the prescriber for a safe alternative.
questions.rationale: Medications, including penicillin, NSAIDs, and anesthetics, are listed triggers of anaphylaxis. Ketorolac is an NSAID like ibuprofen, so giving it to a client whose ibuprofen reaction included throat swelling risks a life-threatening reaction. Substituting acetaminophen is tempting because it seems like a safe fix, but changing the drug requires a prescription. The nurse holds the drug and clarifies the order with the prescriber.
questions.takeaway: Before giving any drug, check the allergy list for the same drug class; hold and clarify if it matches a known trigger.
questions.hintContent: Identify the drug class of the new prescription.
questions.hintStrategy: When an order conflicts with a documented allergy, the safest action is to hold and clarify, not to modify how it is given.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 47-year-old client is being observed after anaphylaxis from shrimp. No further food has been eaten since 1300. Refer to the Vital Signs. Which action should the nurse take first at 1630?
options: Give the prescribed oral cetirizine for the generalized itching
Recheck the vital signs in 15 minutes to confirm the trend
Give epinephrine IM per protocol and call the rapid response team
Notify the provider that the planned discharge should be postponed
optionRationales: Incorrect. An antihistamine treats itching but not the airway narrowing or falling BP.
Incorrect. Waiting delays epinephrine while the client deteriorates.
Correct. Returning hypotension, wheezing, and falling SpO₂ signal a biphasic reaction that needs epinephrine now.
Incorrect. Delaying discharge is appropriate, but treatment of the reaction comes first.
questions.rationale: The 1330 data show a good response to epinephrine, but at 1630 the BP is falling, the HR and RR are rising, wheezing is new, and the SpO₂ has dropped, with no new exposure. This is a second-wave (biphasic) reaction, which is why clients are observed for hours after anaphylaxis. It is treated like the first wave, with epinephrine IM and a call for help. The antihistamine is tempting because itching is one of the new symptoms, but it cannot reverse airway narrowing or hypotension.
questions.takeaway: A biphasic anaphylactic reaction is treated like the first: epinephrine IM and call for help.
questions.hintContent: Compare 1630 with 1330 and decide whether the reaction has returned.
questions.hintStrategy: Trend the data across time; a return of airway and circulation signs calls for the first-line action again.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: In an outpatient clinic, a 24-year-old client develops generalized hives, wheezing, and dizziness 5 minutes after receiving IM penicillin G benzathine. The clinic has a standing order for epinephrine for suspected anaphylaxis. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give diphenhydramine IM and observe the client for 15 minutes
Give epinephrine IM per the standing order while a coworker calls 911
Have the client lie down and take vital signs every 15 minutes
Call the client's primary care provider for further orders
optionRationales: Incorrect. Antihistamines are second-line and do not reverse wheezing or hypotension.
Correct. Outside the hospital, the priorities are epinephrine and EMS activation at the same time.
Incorrect. Positioning and monitoring help, but delaying epinephrine is dangerous.
Incorrect. The standing order already permits epinephrine; calling delays treatment.
questions.rationale: Skin, airway, and circulation are involved minutes after a drug exposure, which is anaphylaxis. In a clinic outside the hospital, the treatment is immediate epinephrine IM plus EMS activation, and delegating the 911 call lets both happen at once. The positioning option is tempting because it includes appropriate care, but it delays the one drug that reverses the reaction. An IM drug cannot be stopped once given, so epinephrine is the first action.
questions.takeaway: Outside the hospital: give epinephrine and activate EMS at once; antihistamines and monitoring come after.
questions.hintContent: Which drug reverses airway narrowing and hypotension?
questions.hintStrategy: When a standing order exists for an emergency, act on it immediately rather than seeking new orders.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A 70-year-old client received IM epinephrine 20 minutes ago for anaphylaxis after a wasp sting. BP is 90/56 mm Hg, and the client reports lightheadedness. The client asks to walk to the bathroom to urinate. Which action is best?
options: Keep the client lying flat and offer a bedpan
Walk the client to the bathroom using a gait belt
Help the client stand at the bedside to use a urinal
Ask the UAP to walk the client to the bathroom
optionRationales: Correct. With a low BP, the client must stay flat; sudden standing can cause collapse.
Incorrect. A gait belt does not prevent collapse from hypotension during anaphylaxis.
Incorrect. Standing with a low BP risks sudden collapse.
Incorrect. The client is unstable and must not walk; delegating the walk adds risk.
questions.rationale: In anaphylaxis, widespread vasodilation and capillary leak reduce the blood volume reaching the organs. A client with a low BP should lie flat with the legs raised and must not stand, walk, or go to the bathroom, because sudden standing can cause collapse. The gait belt is tempting because it seems to make walking safe, but it cannot prevent a hypotensive collapse. A bedpan meets the client's need while maintaining safety.
questions.takeaway: A hypotensive client with anaphylaxis stays flat; use a bedpan, never a walk to the bathroom.
questions.hintContent: Consider what standing does to blood pressure in a client with widespread vasodilation.
questions.hintStrategy: Meet the client's need in the way that does not compromise circulation.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 29-year-old client with a bee-sting allergy is learning to use an epinephrine auto-injector. The client asks, “Why do I have to inject it into my thigh instead of my arm?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “The thigh has fewer nerves, so the injection hurts less there.”
“The thigh is easy for you to reach, even when you are alone.”
“The large thigh muscle absorbs the drug faster than the arm or skin.”
“The thigh can be injected quickly right through your clothing.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Clients often worry about pain, but comfort is not why the thigh is chosen.
Incorrect. The thigh is easy to reach, which helps, but the main reason is how quickly the drug is absorbed there.
Correct. The mid-anterolateral thigh absorbs IM epinephrine faster than a deltoid or subcutaneous injection, and speed saves lives.
Incorrect. Injecting through clothing is allowed and saves time, but it is not why the thigh is preferred over the arm.
questions.rationale: Epinephrine is given IM into the mid-anterolateral (middle of the outer) thigh because the large muscle absorbs the drug faster than a subcutaneous or deltoid injection. Speed matters because deaths in anaphylaxis occur most often when epinephrine is given too late. The less-pain option is tempting because clients often worry about injection pain, but it is not the reason. The auto-injector can also be given through clothing, which saves time.
questions.takeaway: Epinephrine goes IM into the mid-anterolateral thigh for the fastest absorption.
questions.hintContent: Why does the speed of epinephrine matter so much in anaphylaxis?
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the explanation that ties the action to its therapeutic purpose.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 36-year-old client received epinephrine 0.5 mg IM at 0902 for anaphylaxis after a peanut exposure. Refer to the data. How should the nurse interpret the client's response?
options: Treatment is working because BP and breathing have improved
The treatment has failed because the hives have not faded
The reaction has resolved, so monitoring can now be stopped
The treatment has failed because faint wheezes remain
optionRationales: Correct. The response is judged mainly by BP and breathing, and both are better.
Incorrect. Hives can persist; they are not the main measure of the response to epinephrine.
Incorrect. Symptoms can return hours later, so monitoring continues.
Incorrect. Wheezing has lessened markedly; continued improvement is expected with monitoring.
questions.rationale: After epinephrine, the nurse judges the response mainly by blood pressure and breathing (SpO₂, work of breathing, and any stridor or wheezing). Here the BP rose, the SpO₂ climbed, wheezing decreased, and the voice cleared, showing the treatment is working. The hives are tempting as a measure because they are visible, but skin signs often lag and do not reflect the life-threatening problems. Monitoring continues because a biphasic reaction can occur.
questions.takeaway: Judge epinephrine's effect by BP and breathing, not by the skin.
questions.hintContent: Which findings reflect the life-threatening parts of anaphylaxis?
questions.hintStrategy: For evaluation items, focus on the outcomes that matter most for survival.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse completes discharge teaching with a 42-year-old client who has two new epinephrine auto-injectors after an anaphylactic reaction to fire ant stings. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I can inject it right through my jeans if I need to.”
“I'll call 911 after I use it, even if I start feeling better.”
“I'll carry both auto-injectors with me all year round.”
“I'll keep one auto-injector in my car's glove compartment.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is accurate; the auto-injector can be given through clothing.
Incorrect. This is accurate; symptoms can return, so EMS is always called.
Incorrect. This is accurate; two auto-injectors should be carried at all times.
Correct. This needs correcting: auto-injectors must be stored at room temperature, not in a hot car.
questions.rationale: Auto-injector teaching includes carrying two at all times, all year, storing them at room temperature, using epinephrine at the first sign of a serious reaction, and calling 911 even if the client feels better. A glove compartment can become very hot, which can damage the drug. The glove-compartment statement is easy to miss because keeping the device handy sounds responsible. Injecting through clothing is correct and saves time.
questions.takeaway: Store epinephrine auto-injectors at room temperature, never in a hot car, and carry two at all times.
questions.hintContent: Consider how heat affects stored medications.
questions.hintStrategy: In 'further teaching' items, find the statement that sounds sensible but contains an unsafe detail.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 65-year-old client is being treated for anaphylaxis after an IV antibiotic. BP is 78/42 mm Hg. The client's husband says, “She isn't bleeding anywhere. Why is her blood pressure so low?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Her heart has been weakened by the antibiotic and cannot pump hard enough.”
“Her vessels have widened and leaked fluid, so less blood is circulating.”
“Her vessels have tightened, so blood cannot get through to her organs.”
“The reaction made her lose fluid through vomiting and diarrhea.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Shock can affect the heart, but the main problem in anaphylaxis is widened, leaky vessels, not a weak heart.
Correct. Widespread vasodilation and capillary leak reduce the effective blood volume reaching the organs.
Incorrect. The vessels are the problem, but in anaphylaxis they widen rather than tighten; epinephrine is given to constrict them.
Incorrect. GI symptoms can occur in anaphylaxis, but fluid shifting out of leaky vessels, not GI loss, causes the sudden drop in BP.
questions.rationale: In anaphylaxis, mast cells release mediators throughout the body. Widespread vasodilation lowers vascular resistance, and capillary leak moves fluid out of the bloodstream into the tissues, so the blood volume reaching the organs falls and shock develops. The heart-weakness option is tempting because the client is in shock, but the problem is the vessels and fluid shift. This is why epinephrine (which constricts vessels) and isotonic IV fluids are used.
questions.takeaway: Anaphylactic hypotension comes from widespread vasodilation plus capillary leak, not from blood loss.
questions.hintContent: Think about what happens to vessels and fluid when mediators are released everywhere.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the explanation that matches the mediator effects you already know from local inflammation.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: During an admission interview, a 57-year-old client describes several reactions. Which statement should the nurse recognize as the strongest indication of a prior anaphylactic reaction?
options: “Penicillin gave me an upset stomach when I took it last year.”
“After a bee sting last summer, my throat closed and I passed out.”
“I sneeze and get itchy, watery eyes whenever I'm around cats.”
“Amoxicillin gave me an itchy, bumpy rash over my whole body.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Penicillin is a common trigger, but an upset stomach alone is a side effect, not anaphylaxis.
Correct. Airway swelling and loss of consciousness after a sting show airway and circulation involvement.
Incorrect. This is a true allergy, but sneezing and itchy eyes are a mild, localized reaction, not anaphylaxis.
Incorrect. A widespread rash is a real drug allergy to document, but skin involvement alone does not show airway or circulatory compromise.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis involves sudden symptoms in two or more body systems, or airway trouble or hypotension alone, after a likely trigger. Throat closing and passing out after a sting reflect airway swelling and circulatory collapse, the hallmark of anaphylaxis. The penicillin statement is tempting because penicillin is a well-known trigger, but an upset stomach alone describes a side effect. The nurse documents the allergy and the type of reaction so the severity is clear.
questions.takeaway: Document the type of reaction: airway or circulation involvement after a trigger indicates anaphylaxis, not a side effect.
questions.hintContent: Which description involves the airway or circulation?
questions.hintStrategy: Separate true allergic reactions from expected side effects by the body systems involved.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 60-year-old hospitalized client develops stridor, generalized hives, and BP 84/50 mm Hg 8 minutes after an IV infusion of ampicillin begins. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Stop the ampicillin infusion
Keep the IV line open with normal saline
Call the rapid response team and stay with the client
Give diphenhydramine IV before giving epinephrine
Give epinephrine IM in the mid-anterolateral thigh as prescribed
Help the client stand to check for orthostatic changes
optionRationales: Correct. Removing the trigger is the first step.
Correct. The IV line will be needed for fluids and drugs.
Correct. Help is needed, and the client must not be left alone.
Incorrect. Antihistamines are second-line and never come before epinephrine.
Correct. Epinephrine is the first-line drug for anaphylaxis.
Incorrect. Standing can cause collapse in a hypotensive client.
questions.rationale: The hospital priority order is to remove the trigger, call for help and stay, give epinephrine IM, then position, give oxygen and IV fluids, and monitor. The IV line is kept open with normal saline because fluids and drugs will be needed. Giving diphenhydramine first is the tempting error, because antihistamines are familiar allergy drugs, but they do not reverse stridor or hypotension. Standing a hypotensive client risks collapse.
questions.takeaway: Anaphylaxis in the hospital: stop the trigger, keep the line open, call for help, and give epinephrine IM; antihistamines come later.
questions.hintContent: Recall the priority order for emergency care in the hospital.
questions.hintStrategy: Select every action in the first steps of the protocol; reject anything that delays epinephrine or adds risk.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: During a preoperative interview, a 48-year-old client shares a health history. Which statements indicate a potential anaphylaxis trigger that the nurse should communicate to the surgical team? Select all that apply.
options: “My lips swelled after I took ibuprofen for a headache.”
“I don't like the taste of milk, so I avoid it.”
“My throat felt tight right after I was put to sleep for a past surgery.”
“I got hives and wheezed when a balloon popped near my face.”
“Codeine has made me nauseated in the past.”
optionRationales: Correct. NSAIDs are a listed trigger, and lip swelling indicates a serious reaction.
Incorrect. A taste preference is not an allergy.
Correct. Anesthetics are a listed trigger, and throat tightness is an airway sign.
Correct. Balloons are often latex, a listed trigger, and the reaction involved two systems.
Incorrect. Nausea from codeine is a side effect, not an anaphylactic reaction.
questions.rationale: The common anaphylaxis triggers are foods, insect stings, medications (such as penicillin, NSAIDs, and anesthetics), and latex. Each correct statement links a listed trigger to a serious reaction: lip swelling with an NSAID, hives and wheezing with latex, and throat tightness with an anesthetic. These must be documented with the type of reaction and communicated so the team can avoid the triggers and set up a latex-safe environment. Codeine nausea is tempting because it is a medication reaction, but it is a side effect, not an allergy.
questions.takeaway: Ask about foods, stings, medications (penicillin, NSAIDs, anesthetics), and latex, and document the type of each reaction.
questions.hintContent: Match each statement to a listed trigger group and a serious reaction.
questions.hintStrategy: Select statements that pair a known trigger with airway, skin, or circulation signs; reject side effects and preferences.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 39-year-old client is stung by a wasp at a soccer game and has signs of anaphylaxis. Which findings indicate involvement of the circulation? Select all that apply.
options: BP 80/50 mm Hg
Wheezing on expiration
HR 128/min and irregular
Itchy wheals on the arms
Dizziness and lightheadedness
Crampy abdominal pain
optionRationales: Correct. Hypotension shows that vasodilation and leak have reduced circulating volume.
Incorrect. Wheezing reflects airway narrowing, not circulation.
Correct. A fast or abnormal rhythm reflects the circulatory response to falling BP.
Incorrect. Wheals reflect skin involvement.
Correct. Poor perfusion of the brain from vasodilation and fluid leak causes dizziness.
Incorrect. Abdominal cramping reflects GI involvement, not circulation.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis signs are grouped by body system. Circulation signs include low BP, a fast or abnormal heart rhythm, dizziness or lightheadedness, and shock, all caused by vasodilation and fluid leak. Wheezing (airway), abdominal cramps (GI), and wheals (skin) are also signs of anaphylaxis, which makes them tempting, but they belong to other systems. Sorting by system helps the nurse recognize when two or more systems are involved.
questions.takeaway: Circulation signs of anaphylaxis: low BP, fast or abnormal rhythm, dizziness, and shock.
questions.hintContent: Sort each finding into airway, circulation, GI, or skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Every option may be a sign of the condition; the stem asks only for one system, so classify before selecting.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client is being observed on a medical unit 3 hours after successful treatment of anaphylaxis. Vital signs have been stable for 2 hours. Which tasks can the nurse delegate to the UAP? Select all that apply.
options: Decide whether the client is ready for discharge
Listen to the client's lungs for new wheezing
Report any new itching, voice change, or trouble breathing right away
Measure and record vital signs at the scheduled intervals
Teach the client how to use the epinephrine auto-injector
Assist the client with a bedpan or urinal as needed
optionRationales: Incorrect. Evaluating readiness for discharge requires RN judgment.
Incorrect. Auscultation is an assessment that the RN must perform.
Correct. Reporting specific observations to the RN is within UAP scope.
Correct. Taking vital signs on a stable client is within UAP scope.
Incorrect. Client teaching is an RN responsibility.
Correct. Assisting with elimination is basic care that can be delegated.
questions.rationale: Once a client is stable, routine tasks such as vital signs, assistance with elimination, and reporting specific observations can be delegated. Because a biphasic reaction can occur, the RN tells the UAP exactly which changes to report immediately. Listening to the lungs is tempting because it targets the same risk, but auscultation is assessment. Teaching and evaluation also stay with the RN.
questions.takeaway: For a stable client after anaphylaxis, delegate vital signs, basic care, and reporting; keep assessment, teaching, and evaluation.
questions.hintContent: Which tasks need clinical judgment?
questions.hintStrategy: Reject options containing assess, teach, or evaluate (or their synonyms) for UAP.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the condition of several clients who were each exposed to a likely trigger within the last 30 minutes. Which clients need epinephrine now? Select all that apply.
options: A client with hives and two episodes of vomiting after eating shrimp
A client with a new hoarse voice after a dose of IV cefazolin, with no hives
A client who feels anxious after a bee sting, with normal vital signs and no other symptoms
A client with mild itching only at the site of an IV antibiotic
A client with BP 82/48 mm Hg after a yellow jacket sting, with no other symptoms
optionRationales: Correct. Two body systems (skin and GI) suddenly involved after a known allergen indicate anaphylaxis.
Correct. Airway trouble after an exposure is enough on its own; hives are not required.
Incorrect. Anxiety with normal findings and no other system involvement does not meet the criteria.
Incorrect. Localized itching at one site, without other systems, is a local reaction.
Correct. Hypotension after an exposure is enough on its own to indicate anaphylaxis.
questions.rationale: Suspect anaphylaxis when symptoms in two or more body systems appear suddenly after a likely trigger, and act on airway trouble or low BP after an exposure even if nothing else is present. Hives are not required, and some clients never develop skin signs. The client with hives and vomiting is often missed because BP and breathing are normal, but skin plus GI involvement after a known allergen calls for epinephrine. A localized itch with no other findings is a local reaction.
questions.takeaway: Give epinephrine for two or more systems after a trigger, or for airway trouble or low BP alone; do not wait for hives.
questions.hintContent: Count the body systems involved for each client, and look for airway or BP problems.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply the rule to each client separately; one strong finding (airway or BP) can be enough.

questions.stem: During allergy skin-prick testing in an outpatient clinic, a 31-year-old client suddenly develops generalized hives, wheezing, and a hoarse voice. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Wipe the allergens off the skin and observe for 15 minutes
Give diphenhydramine and monitor the breathing closely
Call 911 and stay with the client until help arrives
Give epinephrine IM per the clinic protocol
optionRationales: Incorrect. Removing the allergen is reasonable, but mediators are already released body-wide, and observing delays epinephrine.
Incorrect. Antihistamines are adjuncts that relieve itching and hives, but they cannot reverse airway swelling.
Incorrect. Emergency help is needed, but calling and waiting delays the one drug that reverses anaphylaxis; give epinephrine first.
Correct. Skin, airway, and voice changes after deliberate allergen exposure indicate anaphylaxis; epinephrine must be given immediately.
questions.rationale: Skin testing deliberately exposes the client to allergens, which is why epinephrine must be immediately available. Generalized hives with wheezing and hoarseness involve the skin and airway, so this is anaphylaxis and requires epinephrine IM right away, with emergency help. Wiping off the allergens is tempting because it seems like removing the trigger, but mediators have already been released body-wide. Calling 911 is needed, but it should not delay epinephrine.
questions.takeaway: Epinephrine must be at hand during allergy skin testing; airway signs during testing mean give it immediately.
questions.hintContent: Why must epinephrine be available whenever allergens are deliberately applied?
questions.hintStrategy: When a diagnostic test causes an emergency, treat the client first; the test results can wait.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client who takes prednisone 20 mg daily for chronic lung disease is 3 days post-op after a bowel resection. The incision is only slightly swollen with no redness, but the client reports that the incisional pain is steadily getting worse. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F). Which action is most appropriate?
options: Report the worsening pain; prednisone can hide signs of infection
Document that the incision shows no signs of a wound infection
Give the prescribed analgesic and reassess the pain in 1 hour
Recheck the temperature in 4 hours before reporting any change
optionRationales: Correct. Corticosteroids suppress inflammation, so a subtle change such as steadily increasing pain may be the only clue to infection.
Incorrect. The incision does look calm, but prednisone can mask redness and swelling, so a visual check alone is misleading.
Incorrect. Treating pain is appropriate, but it does not address why pain is worsening, and the change still needs to be reported.
Incorrect. Trending the temperature is reasonable, but steroids can blunt fever, so waiting for it to rise delays evaluation.
questions.rationale: Steroids and NSAIDs suppress the inflammatory response and can hide fever, redness, and swelling, so a client taking them may show only subtle changes. Expected incisional pain eases over the first few days; pain that steadily increases needs follow-up. Documenting 'no signs of infection' is the tempting error because the incision looks calm, but the medication may be masking the classic signs. The nurse reports the change so the provider can evaluate the wound.
questions.takeaway: In clients taking steroids, subtle changes such as increasing pain may be the only sign of infection; report them.
questions.hintContent: Ask how this client's medication changes the classic signs of inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: When the stem includes a drug that suppresses inflammation, read 'normal-looking' findings with suspicion.
