questions.stem: A 51-year-old client is admitted with cellulitis of the right forearm and will start IV antibiotics. Vital signs are stable. Which nursing action is most important for detecting whether the inflammation is spreading on later shifts?
options: Compare the affected arm with the other forearm each shift
Ask the client each shift whether the arm looks any worse
Outline the redness with a skin marker and note the date and time
Check the WBC count each morning to look for a rising trend
optionRationales: Incorrect. Comparing sides is useful, but without a marked border, nurses cannot tell exactly how far the redness has moved.
Incorrect. Involving the client is good, but subjective impressions cannot replace an objective, measurable border.
Correct. A marked, dated border lets every nurse see at a glance whether the redness is spreading or shrinking.
Incorrect. The WBC reflects the systemic response, but it does not show whether the local redness is spreading.
questions.rationale: Good assessment technique makes findings useful to the next nurse. Measuring the area of redness and outlining its border with a skin marker, noting the date and time, creates an objective baseline. On later shifts, redness within the line shows the treatment is working, and redness past it shows spread that needs reporting. Asking the client is tempting because it involves the client, but subjective impressions cannot replace an objective, measurable border.
questions.takeaway: Outline and date the border of cellulitis so spread or improvement can be measured objectively.
questions.hintContent: How can the nurse make today's finding comparable tomorrow?
questions.hintStrategy: For monitoring questions, choose the action that creates an objective, repeatable measurement.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old client with cellulitis of the lower leg reports new numbness and tingling in the toes of the affected foot. The leg is markedly swollen. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Elevate the leg above heart level and reassess in 1 hour
Notify the provider of the new numbness right away
Document the numbness as an expected finding with severe cellulitis
Check pulses, capillary refill, and sensation in both feet
optionRationales: Incorrect. Elevation is part of cellulitis care, but it acts before assessing circulation and may reduce flow if arterial supply is compromised.
Incorrect. Reporting is needed, but the nurse first gathers pulses, capillary refill, and sensation to give the provider complete data.
Incorrect. Swelling is expected with cellulitis, but new numbness and tingling are not and may signal neurovascular compromise.
Correct. Swelling can compress vessels and nerves, so circulation and sensation beyond the site are assessed and compared with the unaffected foot first.
questions.rationale: Swelling from inflammation can squeeze the vessels and nerves beyond the site, so assessment of an inflamed limb includes checking pulses, color, warmth, capillary refill, movement, and sensation, and comparing with the other side. New numbness and tingling are cues of possible neurovascular compromise. Documenting it as expected is the tempting error, because swelling is expected with cellulitis, but numbness is not. The nurse assesses first, then reports abnormal findings.
questions.takeaway: With a swollen, inflamed limb, check circulation and sensation beyond the site and compare with the other side.
questions.hintContent: What can severe swelling do to the structures beyond the inflamed area?
questions.hintStrategy: When a new finding appears, assess it fully before acting on or dismissing it.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old client is admitted with an infected diabetic foot ulcer. The night nurse documented, “WBC normal; no action needed.” Refer to the Laboratory Results and Vital Signs. Which action should the day nurse take first?
options: Agree that the normal WBC rules out an acute bacterial infection
Repeat the CBC in 24 hours before reporting
Report the elevated bands and systemic signs to the provider
Recheck the temperature in 4 hours to see if it falls
optionRationales: Incorrect. A normal total WBC does not rule out infection; the differential shows a left shift.
Incorrect. Waiting delays treatment of a likely spreading infection.
Correct. The high bands show a left shift, and the fever, HR, and RR meet systemic cutoffs, even though the total WBC is normal.
Incorrect. Rechecking delays reporting of findings that already meet systemic criteria.
questions.rationale: A normal total WBC does not rule out infection, so the nurse always reads the differential. Bands of 16% (normal 0–5%) indicate a left shift, meaning the marrow is releasing young neutrophils to fight an acute bacterial infection. The temperature above 38.5 °C, HR above 90, and RR above 20 also meet the systemic cutoffs. Accepting the night nurse's note is tempting because the total WBC is in range, but it ignores both the differential and the vital signs.
questions.takeaway: Always read the differential: increased bands mean a left shift even when the total WBC is normal.
questions.hintContent: Look past the total WBC to the parts of the differential.
questions.hintStrategy: Do not accept a colleague's interpretation without checking the data yourself.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is receiving IV antibiotics for an infected abdominal surgical wound. Refer to the Trend. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Document that ESR changes slowly, so no change in care is needed
Report that the rising CRP suggests the treatment is not working
Continue the current plan because CRP is mainly a cardiac risk marker
Wait for the day 7 results before contacting the provider
optionRationales: Incorrect. The slow-changing ESR does not explain a rising CRP, which normally falls quickly with effective treatment.
Correct. CRP falls quickly when treatment works; a steadily rising CRP with worsening fever signals that the inflammation is not resolving.
Incorrect. CRP is also used to monitor treatment of inflammation.
Incorrect. Three rising values already show a clear trend that needs reporting.
questions.rationale: ESR and CRP show that inflammation is present but not where or why; their value lies in trends. CRP rises within hours and falls quickly when treatment works, while ESR lags and can stay high for weeks. Here the CRP rises on each check along with the fever, so the infection is not responding to the antibiotics. The ESR-lags option is tempting because it is a true fact, but it would only explain a high ESR alongside a falling CRP, not a rising CRP.
questions.takeaway: A falling CRP means treatment is working; a rising CRP during treatment means report it.
questions.hintContent: Which marker responds quickly to effective treatment?
questions.hintStrategy: Distinguish a true statement from one that actually explains the data in front of you.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A UAP reports observations on four postoperative clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client on post-op day 2 with foul-smelling drainage who says, “I feel hot and shaky”
A client on post-op day 1 whose incision has narrow pink edges along the sutures
A client on post-op day 2 with a small amount of pink-tinged drainage on the dressing
A client on post-op day 3 with mild incisional tenderness who is asking for pain medicine
optionRationales: Correct. Purulent drainage plus feeling hot and shaky suggests wound infection that may be becoming systemic.
Incorrect. Narrow pink edges along a closed incision are expected inflammation during healing.
Incorrect. Scant serosanguineous drainage is expected in early healing.
Incorrect. Mild tenderness in the first few days is expected; pain relief is needed but is not the most urgent.
questions.rationale: Some inflammation is expected at a new incision: narrow pink edges, mild swelling and tenderness, and scant serous or serosanguineous drainage. Thick, cloudy, or foul-smelling drainage suggests wound infection, and feeling hot and shaky raises concern for fever and a spreading, systemic response. The client asking for pain medicine is tempting because pain needs a timely response, but mild tenderness is expected and stable. The RN assesses the client with possible infection first.
questions.takeaway: Purulent drainage with systemic symptoms outranks expected signs of incisional healing.
questions.hintContent: Separate the expected signs of healing from those that need follow-up.
questions.hintStrategy: In 'assess first' items, eliminate findings described as expected for the post-op day.

questions.stem: During an admission interview for a 49-year-old client with a painful, swollen knee, the nurse asks about the client's medications. The client asks, “Why do you need to know that I take ibuprofen and prednisone?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Some medicines can cause allergic reactions, so I need a full list.”
“Your provider needs the list to choose safe pain medicine doses.”
“They can hide fever and swelling, so I need to know to interpret my findings.”
“It is routine to ask every client about all medicines they take.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Screening for drug allergies is a valid reason, but it does not explain why these two drugs matter for assessing the knee.
Incorrect. This is a reasonable use of the list, but it misses how these drugs affect the nurse's assessment findings.
Correct. Steroids and NSAIDs suppress inflammation and can mask its signs, which changes how the nurse interprets findings.
Incorrect. Medication history is routine, but this does not explain the purpose, so it misses a chance to build trust.
questions.rationale: Each interview question has a reason. Asking about medications matters because steroids and NSAIDs can hide fever and swelling, and some drugs cause allergic reactions. A client taking both may look less inflamed than the problem truly is. The allergy option is tempting because it is a true reason to ask, but it does not explain why these two drugs matter here. Explaining the purpose builds trust and supports accurate data collection.
questions.takeaway: Ask about steroids and NSAIDs in every inflammation assessment because they can mask the classic signs.
questions.hintContent: How could these two drugs change what the nurse sees and measures?
questions.hintStrategy: For 'best response' items, choose the answer that is both accurate and explains the clinical purpose.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client reports increasing fatigue. Her mother and sister both have Hashimoto thyroiditis. The client asks which screening test would be appropriate. Which test should the nurse expect the provider to order?
options: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Antinuclear antibody (ANA)
Serum protein electrophoresis
optionRationales: Correct. TSH is the screening test that helps detect Hashimoto thyroiditis, an autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid.
Incorrect. ESR shows that inflammation is present, but it is nonspecific and cannot identify the thyroid as the source.
Incorrect. ANA screens for systemic autoimmune disease such as lupus, but it does not measure thyroid function.
Incorrect. Protein electrophoresis shows abnormal blood protein patterns, but it is not used to screen for thyroid disease.
questions.rationale: TSH is the screening test that helps detect Hashimoto thyroiditis, an autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid gland. A family history of thyroid disease plus fatigue makes this client a good candidate for TSH screening. ESR and ANA are tempting because they relate to inflammation and autoimmunity, but they are nonspecific or aimed at other diseases and do not show how the thyroid is working. Matching the test to the suspected condition is the key skill.
questions.takeaway: TSH screens for Hashimoto thyroiditis; ESR and CRP are nonspecific.
questions.hintContent: Which test points to a specific organ rather than inflammation in general?
questions.hintStrategy: Reject nonspecific tests when the stem points to a specific organ or condition.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with no signs of infection has had a mildly elevated CRP on three routine checks over a year. The client asks, “Why did my provider mention my heart when we talked about this test?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “CRP is made by the liver whenever there is inflammation in the body.”
“A high CRP shows inflammation but cannot tell where it is coming from.”
“CRP rises quickly with infection and falls when treatment is working.”
“Ongoing low-grade inflammation, shown by CRP, is linked to heart disease.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is true, but it does not explain why the provider connected the client's CRP to the heart.
Incorrect. CRP is nonspecific, which is true, but this does not answer the client's question about the heart.
Incorrect. This describes CRP's use in monitoring treatment, but the client has no infection, and it does not address heart risk.
Correct. CRP is a cardiac risk marker because persistent low-grade inflammation is linked to heart disease.
questions.rationale: CRP is a protein made by the liver in response to inflammation. It has three main uses: showing that inflammation is present, monitoring treatment, and serving as a cardiac risk marker, because persistent low-grade inflammation is linked to heart disease. The other true facts about CRP are tempting, but only the cardiac risk link answers the client's question. Explaining this accurately helps the client understand the value of modifying cardiac risk factors.
questions.takeaway: CRP is a liver protein that marks inflammation, tracks treatment, and serves as a cardiac risk marker.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three uses of CRP.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that overstate what a nonspecific test can show.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse in a rheumatology clinic is reviewing ESR results for four new clients with joint pain. Refer to the ESR Results. Which client's result indicates active inflammation?
options: Client 1, the 35-year-old woman with an ESR of 18 mm/hr
Client 2, the 40-year-old man with an ESR of 22 mm/hr
Client 3, the 50-year-old man with an ESR of 12 mm/hr
Client 4, the 28-year-old woman with an ESR of 9 mm/hr
optionRationales: Incorrect. The normal range for women is 0–20 mm/hr, so 18 mm/hr is normal.
Correct. The normal range for men is 0–15 mm/hr, so 22 mm/hr is elevated.
Incorrect. 12 mm/hr is within the normal range for men.
Incorrect. 9 mm/hr is within the normal range for women.
questions.rationale: ESR measures how fast red blood cells settle in a tube; inflammation makes them clump and fall faster, so a higher ESR means active inflammation. The normal ranges differ by sex: 0–15 mm/hr for men and 0–20 mm/hr for women. Client 1 is the tempting choice because 18 is close to 22, but it is normal for a woman. The ESR is nonspecific, so an elevated result shows that inflammation is present but not its cause.
questions.takeaway: ESR normal: men 0–15 mm/hr, women 0–20 mm/hr; interpret by the client's sex.
questions.hintContent: Check whether the normal range is the same for every client.
questions.hintStrategy: When lab values look similar, look for a client characteristic that changes the reference range.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old client with systemic lupus erythematosus is having a flare. The provider orders a chemistry panel that includes creatinine, liver enzymes, and muscle enzymes. The client asks why so many tests are needed. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “They check for side effects of the medicines used to treat lupus.”
“They show whether inflammation is affecting your kidneys, liver, or muscles.”
“They show how much inflammation is present in your body right now.”
“They help confirm that your current symptoms are caused by lupus.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. These tests can monitor drug effects, but during a flare they are ordered to see whether inflammation is reaching organs.
Correct. Chemistry panels show whether widespread inflammation is injuring organs such as the kidneys, liver, and muscles.
Incorrect. Measuring inflammation level is the role of ESR and CRP; chemistry panels show organ injury instead.
Incorrect. Lupus is diagnosed with other tests and findings; chemistry panels show organ involvement rather than confirm the disease.
questions.rationale: Widespread inflammation, as in an SLE flare, can injure organs, so chemistry panels help the team see how far the damage reaches: creatinine for the kidneys, liver enzymes for the liver, and muscle enzymes for muscle. Other tests, such as the ESR and protein electrophoresis (increased gamma globulin and decreased albumin), support the picture of active SLE. The 'confirms the diagnosis' option is tempting because many tests are being run, but chemistry panels show organ involvement rather than diagnose the disease.
questions.takeaway: Chemistry panels show whether inflammation is affecting the kidneys, liver, or muscles.
questions.hintContent: What does each part of the panel measure?
questions.hintStrategy: Match the test to its purpose; reject options that describe a different test.

questions.stem: During an admission interview, a 59-year-old client with a slow-healing foot wound shares health information. Which statements are cues that may affect inflammation or wound healing? Select all that apply.
options: “I eat fast food most days and rarely eat vegetables.”
“I take prednisone every day for my lungs.”
“I had my tonsils removed when I was 6 years old.”
“I walk my dog for 30 minutes every day.”
“I've had diabetes for 20 years.”
optionRationales: Correct. A Western diet promotes inflammation, and poor nutrition slows repair.
Correct. Steroids suppress inflammation and can hide signs of infection.
Incorrect. A remote childhood procedure is not a recent break in the skin.
Incorrect. Regular activity is a healthy behavior, not a risk to healing.
Correct. Diabetes slows healing and is an important chronic condition to note.
questions.rationale: Interview questions about chronic conditions, medications, diet, recent procedures, fatigue, appetite, and stress each have a purpose. Diabetes slows healing, prednisone can hide fever and redness, and a Western diet promotes inflammation while poor protein and vitamin C intake slow repair. The tonsillectomy is tempting because the nurse asks about procedures, but the concern is recent procedures, which create a door for infection. Daily walking supports health.
questions.takeaway: Interview for chronic conditions, medications, diet, and recent procedures because each changes inflammation or healing.
questions.hintContent: Think about why each interview question is asked.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the time frame: 'recent' procedures matter; remote ones usually do not.

questions.stem: The nurse is performing a focused physical assessment of a 44-year-old client with an acutely inflamed right knee. Which techniques should the nurse use? Select all that apply.
options: Compare the right knee with the left knee
Check pulses, capillary refill, and sensation below the knee
Measure and document the size of the swollen area
Assess only the right knee to avoid tiring the client
Massage the knee firmly to find the most tender area
optionRationales: Correct. Comparing sides shows how much the inflamed joint differs from normal.
Correct. Swelling can compress vessels and nerves beyond the site.
Correct. Measurements let the next nurse tell whether swelling is increasing or decreasing.
Incorrect. Without comparison, the nurse cannot judge how abnormal the findings are.
Incorrect. Firm massage causes pain and can worsen inflammation.
questions.rationale: Good technique makes findings useful: measure the area of redness or swelling, compare with the other side, and check circulation beyond the site (pulses, color, warmth, capillary refill, movement, and sensation). These steps allow the team to trend findings and detect compression. Assessing only the affected knee is tempting because it seems efficient, but without a comparison the nurse cannot tell how much the joint has changed. Gentle palpation, not firm massage, is used to assess tenderness.
questions.takeaway: Assess an inflamed site by measuring, comparing with the other side, and checking circulation beyond it.
questions.hintContent: How will the next nurse know whether the knee is better or worse?
questions.hintStrategy: Select techniques that produce objective, comparable data and protect the client.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse assesses the incision of a 67-year-old client on postoperative day 2 after a total knee replacement. Which findings are expected signs of normal healing? Select all that apply.
options: Incisional pain that has increased each day since surgery
A narrow pink border about 2 mm wide along the closed incision
Mild swelling and tenderness that are easing compared with yesterday
A scant amount of pink-tinged drainage on the dressing
Red streaks extending up the thigh from the incision
Thick, cloudy drainage with a foul odor
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pain that increases over time instead of easing needs follow-up.
Correct. A few millimeters of pink or red along a closed incision is expected inflammation.
Correct. Mild swelling and tenderness that ease over the first few days are expected.
Correct. Scant serosanguineous drainage is expected early in healing.
Incorrect. Red streaks moving away from a wound suggest spreading infection.
Incorrect. Purulent drainage suggests a wound infection.
questions.rationale: A new incision normally shows some inflammation: narrow pink or red edges of a few millimeters, mild swelling and tenderness that ease over the first few days, and scant serous or serosanguineous drainage. Findings that need follow-up include redness spreading outward or red streaks, thick, cloudy, or foul-smelling drainage, and swelling or pain that increase over time. Increasing pain is the tempting choice because some pain is expected after surgery, but the trend, not the presence of pain, is the cue.
questions.takeaway: Expected: narrow pink edges, easing tenderness, scant serosanguineous drainage. Follow-up: streaks, pus, and worsening pain.
questions.hintContent: Picture the difference between expected healing and early infection.
questions.hintStrategy: Pay attention to trend words such as 'easing' and 'increased each day.'

questions.stem: A 26-year-old client with recurrent hives is scheduled for allergy skin testing next week. Which teaching points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Stop antihistamines for several days before the test, as the allergist directs
Epinephrine will be ready in the room during the test
The same test will also screen you for thyroid disease
The results help identify allergens you can then avoid
Take your usual antihistamine the morning of the test to prevent itching
optionRationales: Correct. Antihistamines block the wheal-and-flare response and can cause false-negative results.
Correct. The client is deliberately exposed to allergens, so epinephrine must be immediately available.
Incorrect. Thyroid screening uses a TSH blood test, not skin testing.
Correct. Skin testing identifies allergens so the client can avoid them.
Incorrect. Taking an antihistamine before testing can block the reaction and give false-negative results.
questions.rationale: Skin testing identifies allergens so the client can avoid them. Antihistamines block the wheal-and-flare reaction, so the client is usually told to stop them for several days before the test, as the allergist directs; otherwise results may be falsely negative. Because allergens are deliberately applied, epinephrine must be immediately available. Taking an antihistamine the morning of the test is tempting because it seems to prevent discomfort, but it defeats the purpose of the test.
questions.takeaway: Before skin testing, hold antihistamines as directed; during testing, keep epinephrine ready.
questions.hintContent: How would an antihistamine change the skin's response to the test allergens?
questions.hintStrategy: For teaching items, check each option for accuracy and for whether it would change the test result.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 86-year-old client with suspected pneumonia takes prednisone daily for COPD, ibuprofen every 6 hours for knee pain, lisinopril for hypertension, and a daily multivitamin. Which factors could hide the classic signs of infection and inflammation in this client? Select all that apply.
options: Lisinopril for hypertension
A daily multivitamin
The client's age of 86 years
Daily prednisone
Ibuprofen every 6 hours
optionRationales: Incorrect. Lisinopril does not suppress the inflammatory response.
Incorrect. A multivitamin does not mask the signs of infection.
Correct. Older adults often present with a low or normal temperature rather than a fever.
Correct. Steroids suppress inflammation and can hide fever, redness, and swelling.
Correct. Around-the-clock NSAIDs lower prostaglandin-driven fever and pain.
questions.rationale: Steroids, NSAIDs, and older age can all hide fever and redness, so subtle changes matter. Older adults may show a low or normal temperature, and a temperature below 36 °C counts as a systemic sign. Prednisone suppresses the inflammatory response, and scheduled ibuprofen blocks the prostaglandins that drive fever and pain. Lisinopril is tempting because it is a daily prescription drug, but it does not mask inflammation.
questions.takeaway: Older age, steroids, and NSAIDs can mask fever and redness; look for subtle changes.
questions.hintContent: Which factors blunt the body's ability to show fever and redness?
questions.hintStrategy: Consider each factor's effect on the inflammatory response, not just whether it is a medication.
